raw.summary: Hono: `css` helper does not escape a closing tag split between the template and an interpolated value, allowing HTML injection
raw.details:
### Summary

The `css` helper in `hono/css` escapes a `/` that follows `<` inside an interpolated value so that a value cannot close the `<style>` element. The check only looks inside each value. When the text before a value ends with `<`, whether that is the template itself or an earlier interpolated value, and the next value starts with `/`, the `/` is not escaped and the combined output contains an unescaped closing tag.

### Details

Interpolated string values are escaped one at a time before they are joined with the surrounding template text. The rule that neutralizes `</` therefore cannot see a `<` that belongs to the template. A template such as a `content` declaration that opens with a literal `<` and interpolates a string right after it produces a raw `</style>` when that string starts with `/style>`. During server-side rendering the `<Style />` element is closed early and the rest of the value is interpreted as HTML.

This issue arises only when `<` is the last character before an interpolation in a `css` template, either written in the template or supplied by a preceding value, and the interpolated value is controlled by a client.

### Impact

A client that controls such a value can inject HTML, including script, into the page rendered on the server.

This may lead to:

- Execution of attacker-controlled script in the browser of a user who views the page
- Exposure of information available to that page

This issue affects applications that interpolate untrusted strings into a `css` template immediately after a `<`, including two adjacent interpolations such as `${prefix}${name}` where both are untrusted. Other uses of the `css` helper are not affected.

### Workarounds

Do not interpolate untrusted values into `css` templates, or make sure the text before an interpolated value does not end with `<`.

raw.summary: OpenTelemetry JavaScript: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File and Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor in @opentelemetry/instrumentation-http
raw.details:
### Summary

`@opentelemetry/instrumentation-http` redacts sensitive URL query parameters on **outgoing (client) spans** but not on **incoming (server) spans**. The server-span path writes the raw query string verbatim into the `url.query` attribute, so credentials embedded in inbound request URLs — AWS presigned-URL signatures, Azure SAS tokens (`sig`), GCS signed-URL signatures — are exported in plaintext to the configured tracing backend.

Configuring the `redactedQueryParams` option **does not change this**, as this applies only to outgoing (client) spans.

### Impact

**Information disclosure / credential leakage** (CWE-200; CWE-532, insertion of sensitive information into telemetry data).

**Who is impacted:** any Node.js service instrumented with `@opentelemetry/instrumentation-http` — directly or transitively via `@opentelemetry/auto-instrumentations-node` — that receives inbound requests carrying credentials in the query string. Common cases: services fronting presigned S3/GCS downloads, Azure SAS-token URLs, and signature-authenticated webhooks.

**Consequence:** clients' still-valid credentials are written into server spans and stored by the tracing backend, readable by anyone with span-read access — observability vendor infrastructure, dashboard users, and internal audiences far broader than the credential's intended scope. Presigned-URL signatures typically remain valid for minutes to days after capture, so this is not merely historical exposure.

**Severity:** Moderate. Exploitation requires read access to the telemetry backend, and inbound URLs must actually carry signed credentials. However, the gap is a documented mitigation that silently fails to apply, which defeats the mitigation operators would reach for.

### Patches

This vulnerability has been patched in `@opentelemetry/instrumentation-http` version `0.222.0`.
Known sensitive query string values (as defined by Semantic Conventions) are redacted by default from span data for incoming spans.
The `redactedQueryParamsServer` configuration option was added for customization.

raw.summary: Hono: `csrf()` does not check requests sent by hyperlink auditing (`text/ping`)
raw.details:
### Summary

`csrf()` validates a request only when its `Content-Type` is one of the three types an HTML form can send. Chromium's hyperlink auditing (`<a ping>`) sends a cross-origin POST with the user's cookies and the content type `text/ping`, which is not in that list. The middleware does not look at `Origin` or `Sec-Fetch-Site` for such a request, so it is passed to the handler.

### Details

The middleware skips the origin check when the content type is not one that a form submission produces. The assumption was that any other content type requires a CORS preflight and therefore cannot be sent cross-origin with credentials. Hyperlink auditing is an exception: Chrome and Edge send the ping as a credentialed POST without a preflight, with a fixed body and `Content-Type: text/ping`.

A page on another origin can therefore trigger a POST to any URL of the application. The `csrf()` options for `origin` and `secFetchSite` do not change the outcome, because neither header is evaluated for the request.

The request body is fixed, so only actions whose effect does not depend on the body can be triggered. Firefox does not send pings by default. As with any CSRF, the user's cookie must be sent with the request, which with the default `SameSite=Lax` means a same-site origin or a cookie set with `SameSite=None`.

### Impact

A user who visits a malicious page in Chrome or Edge while logged in to an application protected by `csrf()` can be made to send a state-changing request to that application, such as logging out, deleting a resource, or toggling a setting that is selected by the path or query string.

This issue affects applications that rely on `csrf()` as their CSRF protection and expose state-changing endpoints whose effect does not depend on the request body.

### Workarounds

Reject requests with a `Content-Type` of `text/ping` in a middleware registered before `csrf()`, or set session cookies with `SameSite=Strict`.

raw.summary: fast-xml-parser: Quadratic CPU consumption scanning unterminated stop-node tags
raw.details:
### Summary

With the non-default stopNodes option, a stop node's body with many "<a " fragments and no closing ">" anywhere after makes readStopNodeData() rescan the entire remaining input from every "<". The failed lookahead is neither cached nor bounded, so n fragments cost O(n²) before the parser throws. Availability-only (CPU exhaustion), needs the non-default stopNodes option — not benchmarked yet, see Proof of Concept.

### Details

**CWE-407** — Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity

**Code**
- `OrderedObjParser.js:520` — `parseXml()` calls `readStopNodeData()` after a matching stop node opens
- `OrderedObjParser.js:810` — calls `readTagExp()` for every non-special `<`
- `OrderedObjParser.js:688-722` — `tagExpWithClosingIndex()` scans to end-of-input and returns `undefined` when no `>` exists
- `OrderedObjParser.js:812-818` — on failure, `i` isn't advanced, so the next `<` repeats the same full scan
- `OrderedObjParser.js:423` — the main parse loop throws immediately on the same failure; only the stop-node path retries

**Root cause:** a failed closing-`>` lookahead is neither cached nor bounded — `n` copies of `<a ` with no later `>` means `n` scans over the remaining input, O(n²) work, before it finally throws.

**Fix**
1. Throw immediately in `readStopNodeData()` when `readTagExp()` returns `undefined`
2. Or break the loop on the first failed scan
3. Or find the next `>` once and reuse/bound that result
4. Add a test asserting near-linear scaling when payload size doubles

### Proof of concept

Not benchmarked — static-analysis finding, confidence 0.5.

To confirm: configure `stopNodes` matching a root element. Build input as `'<stop>' + '<a '.repeat(n)`. Time `parse()` until it throws `Unexpected end of <tag>`. Start around n=10,000 and double it — quadratic should show ~4x time per doubling, linear ~2x. Control: same input with a `>` present, or `stopNodes` unset.

### Impact

CPU-exhaustion DoS in Node.js services parsing untrusted XML with `stopNodes` enabled. A ~100KB payload is estimated at ~10⁹ character operations (roughly a second or more of blocked event loop) — analytical estimate, not a benchmark. No confidentiality/integrity impact. CVSS 3.1: `AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L` (3.7, Low).

raw.summary: Hono: `validator('form')` skips validation for `multipart/form-data` requests with extra parameters
raw.details:
### Summary

`validator('form')` only recognizes a `multipart/form-data` `Content-Type` that carries nothing but a single `boundary` parameter. A request with another legal parameter, such as `charset`, or with extra whitespace after the `;` is not recognized as a form. The validation callback then receives an empty object, while `c.req.parseBody()` still parses the body as a form.

### Details

The check that decides whether a request body is a form was written as a strict pattern over the whole `Content-Type` value. Any parameter list that does not look exactly like `; boundary=...` fails the check. When it fails, the middleware does not read the body and passes an empty object to the validation callback. If the callback accepts an empty object, the request proceeds to the handler, which can still read all submitted fields through `c.req.parseBody()` or `c.req.formData()`.

`application/x-www-form-urlencoded` is not affected. Only the `multipart/form-data` branch has the strict pattern.

This issue arises when an application relies on `validator('form')` to reject or restrict fields and the validation callback does not fail on an empty object.

### Impact

An unauthenticated client can send form fields that the `form` validator never sees, by adding a legal parameter to the `Content-Type` header.

This may lead to:

- Allow-list or required-field checks in the validator being skipped
- Fields the application intended to reject reaching the handler

This issue affects applications that use `validator('form')` with `multipart/form-data` requests and whose validation callback accepts an empty object.

### Workarounds

Reject an empty object in the `validator('form')` callback, or validate the result of `await c.req.parseBody()` in the handler.

raw.summary: Hono: `mount()` and `app.mount()` can forward a path that bypasses middleware scoped inside the mount prefix
raw.details:
### Summary

`mount()` and `app.mount()` remove the mount prefix from the request path and forward the rest to the mounted application. Two mistakes in that step let a crafted request reach a route of the mounted application that the outer application protects with path-scoped middleware, such as an authentication check on `/app/admin/*`. The outer application routes on the original path, so the middleware does not run.

### Details

1. **Dynamic prefix** (all affected versions): for a mount such as `/api/:tenant/*`, the prefix was removed by the length of the route pattern, not of the matched prefix. A request with a longer or shorter first segment is cut in the middle, so `/api/a/xxxxx/admin/secret` reaches the mounted application as `/admin/secret`.
2. **Re-normalization** (since 4.12.21): the forwarded path was built from the decoded request path and assigned to `url.pathname`, which turns a decoded backslash into `/` and collapses `..`. `/app/public%5C..%5Cadmin/secret` reaches the mounted application as `/admin/secret`.

The fix removes the prefix segment by segment from the raw pathname, using the matched parameter values for its length. Route patterns that cannot be handled safely now throw: duplicate parameter names and a wildcard inside the last segment such as `/assets*`. A trailing slash in an `app.mount()` prefix no longer removes an extra segment.

### Impact

An unauthenticated client can reach a route of a mounted application that the outer application protects with path-scoped middleware.

This affects applications that use `mount()` or `app.mount()` and rely on middleware registered on a sub-path inside the mount prefix for authentication or authorization.

### Workarounds

Register the authentication middleware inside the mounted application.

raw.summary: Forge: Ed25519 signature verification accepts small-order public keys
raw.details:
### Summary
`ed25519.verify()` does not reject public keys of small order, such as the identity point. Under such a key, a signature with `S = 0` and a small-order `R` verifies for many messages, or for every message with the identity key, without any private key. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

### Details
`crypto_sign_open()` in `lib/ed25519.js` decodes the public key `A` with `unpackneg()`, which only checks that the point is on the curve, and then checks `R == [S]B - [k]A` with `k = SHA-512(R || A || M)`. Nothing rejects public keys of small order: the identity point, the other 7 points of order 2, 4 or 8, and their non-canonical encodings with `y >= p`.

With `S = 0`, the check becomes `R == [k](-A)`. For a small-order `A`, `[k](-A)` is one of at most 8 small-order points, so an attacker can make a valid signature by trying the small-order values of `R`. For the identity key (`01 00 … 00`), `R = identity` and `S = 0` verifies for every message. For the other small-order keys, a given message can be forged with high probability. No private key is involved. The `S < L` check added for CVE-2026-33895 (GHSA-q67f-28xg-22rw) doesn't apply, because `S = 0` is canonical.

Keys produced by Ed25519 key generation (`ed25519.generateKeyPair()` or any RFC 8032 implementation) are never small-order, so signatures under them cannot be forged this way. Applications are affected when they verify signatures against a public key an attacker can choose (for example a key included with the signed data, a self-registered key, or a key in an attacker-controlled document) and rely on the signature being bound to the message: proof of possession, attribution, non-repudiation or deduplication.

RFC 8032 doesn't require rejecting small-order public keys, and implementations differ. libsodium rejects them, and Node.js `crypto.verify()` (OpenSSL) rejects these signatures.

The fix rejects a public key `A` when `[8]A` is the identity point. This covers all small-order points and their non-canonical encodings.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3. `ed25519.verify()` returns `false` for small-order public keys.

#### Workarounds
Before calling `ed25519.verify()` with a public key from untrusted input, reject keys whose 32-byte encoding is one of the small-order points (the identity `01 00 … 00` and the other encodings that libsodium blocks), or only verify against keys you generated or have otherwise validated.

#### Resources
- RFC 8032, Section 5.1.7 (Ed25519 verification): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8032#section-5.1.7
- GHSA-q67f-28xg-22rw / CVE-2026-33895 (a different Ed25519 verification issue, fixed in 1.4.0): https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-q67f-28xg-22rw

#### Severity
CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N (3.7, Low)
CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (6.3)
CVSS 4.0 rates this Moderate because its integrity weighting is higher; the severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.

#### Credits
Reported by @analisaperlengkapan.

### Proof of concept
Identity public key `A = 01 00 … 00` (32 bytes) and signature `R = 01 00 … 00`, `S = 00 … 00` (64 bytes):

    forge.ed25519.verify({message: 'admin=true', encoding: 'utf8',
      signature: SIG, publicKey: IDENTITY});
    // <= 1.4.2: true for any message; node:crypto.verify(): false
    // 1.4.3: false

Other small-order public keys (orders 2, 4 and 8, and non-canonical encodings) give forgeries for many messages with `S = 0` and a small-order `R`.

Regression tests are in tests/unit/ed25519.js, and the reporter's PoC is in tests/pocs/ghsa-6889-vf6x-f3g5.js.

### Impact
Applications that verify Ed25519 signatures with node-forge against a public key that an attacker can choose are affected. An attacker can provide a small-order public key and then produce signatures that verify for many or all messages without a private key, defeating checks that rely on a signature being bound to its message under that key (proof of possession, attribution, non-repudiation, deduplication). Signatures under keys from honest key generation cannot be forged, and applications that only verify against their own or otherwise trusted keys are not affected.

raw.summary: Forge: ReDoS in forge.http response header and cookie trimming
raw.details:
`forge.http` trims response header and `Set-Cookie` values with the regular expression `/\s*$/`, which takes quadratic time on a long run of whitespace followed by another character. A server or on-path attacker can block a `forge.http` client for minutes with one large response header. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

### Details
`_trimString()` in `lib/http.js` removes trailing whitespace with `str.replace(/\s*$/, '')`. On a string of n whitespace characters followed by a non-whitespace character, the regular expression engine tries a match at each of the n positions and scans the rest of the run each time, so the work is O(n^2). `forge.http` calls `_trimString()` on every response header value read by `response.readHeader()`, and again on cookie names and values in `response.getCookies()`. There is no limit on header size.

With Node.js 24, an 80 KB header value takes about 4 seconds to parse, and 1 MB about 10 minutes, during which the event loop (or browser tab) is blocked.

`forge.http` is not loaded by `require('node-forge')`. It is part of the `forge.all` bundle and needs a socket pool provided by the application (historically Flash sockets via `forge.xhr`), so few applications use it.

The fix trims trailing whitespace with a loop, as `lib/pem.js` has done since 1.4.1. The trimmed result is unchanged.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

#### Workarounds
Limit the size of HTTP response headers before passing them to `forge.http`, for example in the socket pool's data handler.

#### Resources
- Related: GHSA-7wch-p9px-956x (ReDoS in PEM decoding, fixed in 1.4.1): https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-7wch-p9px-956x

#### Severity
CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H (5.9, Moderate)
CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (8.2)
CVSS 4.0 has no counterpart to 3.1's AC:H beyond AT:P and scores this higher; the severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.

#### Credits
Reported by @manus-pi.

### Proof of concept
    var response = forge.http.createResponse();
    var ws = new Array(40001).join('\t ');
    response.readHeader(forge.util.createBuffer(
      'HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nX-A: a' + ws + 'X\r\n\r\n'));
    // <= 1.4.2: about 4 seconds (quadratic in the whitespace length)
    // 1.4.3: about 1 ms

Regression tests are in tests/security/ghsa-6cv4-p8m7-4r25.js.

### Impact
Applications that use `forge.http` to talk to servers they don't control are affected. The server, or an on-path attacker, can send a response header that blocks the client's event loop for minutes, denying service to everything else in the process. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact.

raw.summary: Signal K Server: Buffered logs exposed to unauthenticated WebSocket clients
Astro: Reflected XSS via unescaped slot names in @astrojs/svelte
raw.details:
## Summary The `@astrojs/svelte` renderer wraps slotted content passed to Svelte components in an `` element, and writes the slot name into its `name` attribute without HTML escaping. A slot name containing `"` could end the attribute and inject arbitrary HTML into the page. For example, a page that takes a slot name from the request: ```astro --- import Tabs from '../components/Tabs.svelte'; const tab = Astro.url.searchParams.get('tab'); ---
…
 ``` rendered with a Svelte 5 component that renders its snippets by name: ```svelte {@render snippets[active]?.()} ``` would output a `tab` value such as `x">` as live HTML. ## Impact Reflected cross-site scripting. An attacker who gets a user to open a crafted link can run JavaScript on the site's origin, but only in applications where all of the following are true: - The page passes request-controlled input (such as a query parameter) as a slot name. - The Svelte component is hydrated with a `client:*` directive. For non-hydrated components the slot wrapper is removed from the output, together with its `name` attribute. - The Svelte component renders the attacker-chosen slot, which in practice means a Svelte 5 component that renders snippets by a dynamic name. Components that never render the slot only output Astro's already escaped fallback template. This is the `@astrojs/svelte` counterpart of GHSA-8hv8-536x-4wqp (CVE-2026-50146), which fixed the same issue in `astro` core. The same unescaped value was also used when hydrating the component in the browser. ## Affected versions `@astrojs/svelte` >= 5.7.3, <= 9.1.1. ## Patches Fixed in `@astrojs/svelte` 9.1.2. Slot names are now HTML-escaped in the server renderer and in the client-side hydration code. ## Workarounds Upgrade to `@astrojs/svelte` 9.1.2 or later. Before upgrading, do not use request-controlled input as a slot name, or map it to a fixed set of known slot names before passing it to a component. ## Credits Reported by @manus-pi.

raw.summary: @grpc/grpc-js: RBAC override configs in VirtualHost and Route resources are not applied
raw.details:
### Summary

`XdsServer` in `@grpc/grpc-js-xds` does not apply `RBACPerRoute` overrides from matching Route or VirtualHost resources. When a trusted xDS control plane supplies a broad top-level ALLOW policy and a stricter override, `XdsServer` ACKs the resources but evaluates the RPC under the top-level policy.

### Details

### Override parser lookup uses the override message type

`parseOverrideFilterConfig()` in packages/grpc-js-xds/src/http-filter.ts:225-257 looks up FILTER_REGISTRY using the override message type:

`type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.rbac.v3.RBACPerRoute`
Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/http-filter.ts#L225-L257

`setup()` in packages/grpc-js-xds/src/http-filter/rbac-filter.ts:167-173 registers the filter only under the top-level RBAC type:

`type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.rbac.v3.RBAC`
Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/http-filter/rbac-filter.ts#L167-L173

The lookup returns null even though the registered entry contains `parseOverrideRbacConfig()`, and server.ts silently skips the override.

### Override maps are keyed by type URL instead of filter name

`overrideConfigMaps` in server.ts:99-102 is documented as keyed by HTTP filter name, but server.ts:169-174 stores each map under `filterConfig.typeUrl`.

Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/server.ts#L99-L102

Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/server.ts#L169-L174

Route overrides are later looked up by their `typed_per_filter_config` key, which is the `HttpFilter.name`. An ordinary key such as rbac therefore misses the stored map.

### VirtualHost overrides are not read

`handleRouteConfigurationResource()` in server.ts:225-249 reads `route.typed_per_filter_config` but never reads `virtualHost.typed_per_filter_config`.

Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/server.ts#L225-L249

When no override reaches the RBAC interceptor, rbac-filter.ts:125-155 evaluates the broader top-level policy.

### Proof of concept

Set:
```
GRPC_XDS_EXPERIMENTAL_RBAC=true
```

Run `XdsServer` with a protected unary handler.

Have the ADS control plane deliver a Listener containing an RBAC HTTP filter named rbac with a top-level ALLOW-any policy:

```
name: rbac
typed_config:
  "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.rbac.v3.RBAC
  rules:
    action: ALLOW
    policies:
      allow-any:
        principals: [{ any: true }]
        permissions: [{ any: true }]
```

Deliver a matching non-forwarding route with this override:

```
typed_per_filter_config:
  rbac:
    "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.rbac.v3.RBACPerRoute
    rbac:
      rules:
        action: DENY
        policies:
          deny-any:
            principals: [{ any: true }]
            permissions: [{ any: true }]
```

Invoke the protected unary method without credentials.

Expected: The route-specific DENY policy rejects the RPC before the protected handler runs.

Observed: `XdsServer` ACKs the resources, retains the top-level ALLOW policy, and runs the protected handler.

```
Listener and RouteConfiguration: ACKED
gRPC status: OK
handler invocations: 1
response: PROTECTED_SECRET_RECORD_RBAC_OVERRIDE
```

### Impact

Users of `@grpc/grpc-js-xds` who are using RBAC-based authentication with override configurations may unintentionally accept some requests that should be rejected.

raw.summary: Hono: RegExpRouter skips wildcard middleware for some route sets and for paths with an encoded line terminator
raw.details:
### Summary

RegExpRouter, which the default `SmartRouter` selects for most applications, skipped wildcard middleware in three cases, so a route handler ran without the middleware registered for it:

1. Middleware whose parameter is written with the explicit default pattern, such as `/api/:tenant{[^/]+}/admin/*`, was not applied to a route written as `/api/:tenant/admin/:id`. (since 4.13.0)
2. Middleware on `/admin/*` was not applied to a route registered on `/admin*` for paths under `/admin/`. (since 4.1.4)
3. For a path with an encoded line terminator (`%0A`, `%0D`, `%E2%80%A8`, `%E2%80%A9`), no wildcard pattern matched, so the request reached the not-found handler without any wildcard middleware. (since 4.4.0)

TrieRouter, LinearRouter and PatternRouter apply the middleware in all three cases.

### Details

RegExpRouter decides at registration time which wildcard middleware covers which route. In cases 1 and 2 it treated patterns that match the same requests as different ones. In case 3 the compiled wildcard did not match line terminators.

The fix derives the coverage from the structure of the registered paths and lets wildcards match line terminators. It also corrects other differences from the other routers (a wildcard in the middle of a path with parameters, duplicate middleware, middleware on static routes), and rejects custom patterns that can match the empty string, such as `{[0-9]*}`, with `UnsupportedPathError`. `PreparedRegExpRouter` data must be regenerated.

### Impact

An unauthenticated client can reach a route handler, or the not-found handler, without the authentication or authorization middleware registered on a wildcard path.

This affects applications that use RegExpRouter, directly or through the default `SmartRouter`, and rely on wildcard middleware for authentication or authorization.

### Workarounds

Use `new Hono({ router: new TrieRouter() })`.

raw.summary: Forge: TLS client crash on a handshake record received without a session
raw.details:
### Summary
A `forge.tls` client throws an uncaught `TypeError` from `connection.process()` when it receives a ServerHello while it has no session: after a `close_notify` alert or a call to `close()`, or before `handshake()` is called. A malicious server or an on-path attacker can use this to terminate a Node.js process. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

### Details
`tls.handleHandshake()` in `lib/tls.js` updates the handshake digests with `c.session.md5.update(bytes)` before it calls the message handler. A client creates its session in `handshake()`, and `c.reset()` sets it to `null` when the connection is closed. Closing doesn't set the fail flag, and the client goes back to expecting a ServerHello, so a Handshake record received afterwards still reaches `handleHandshake()`, which throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'md5')`.

This happens:
- after the server sends a `close_notify` alert (at any alert level);
- after the application calls `close()`;
- before the application calls `handshake()`.

The exception propagates out of `connection.process()`. Applications that pass socket data to `process()` from a `data` event handler without catching exceptions, as in the README example, terminate. After a reset the connection uses no encryption, so an on-path attacker can inject the records even when the real server is honest.

Servers are not affected: a server creates its session when it receives a ClientHello.

The fix handles these records like other unexpected records on a closed client: they are ignored.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

#### Workarounds
Catch exceptions thrown by `connection.process()` and close the socket, or stop passing socket data to `process()` once the `closed` callback has been called and until `handshake()` is called again.

#### Resources
- RFC 5246, section 7.2.1 (Closure Alerts): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5246#section-7.2.1
- Related: GHSA-525v-9gp9-w22h (another TLS client `TypeError`, fixed in 1.4.1): https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-525v-9gp9-w22h

#### Severity
CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H (5.9, Moderate)
CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (8.2)
CVSS 4.0 has no counterpart to 3.1's AC:H beyond AT:P and scores this higher; the severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.

#### Credits
Reported by @manus-use.

### Proof of concept
    var c = forge.tls.createConnection({server: false, ...});
    c.handshake();
    // warning close_notify alert, then an empty ServerHello, in separate
    // process() calls
    c.process(forge.util.hexToBytes('15030100020100'));
    c.process(forge.util.hexToBytes('160301000402000000'));
    // <= 1.4.2: TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'md5')
    // 1.4.3: the record is ignored

The reporter's PoC is in tests/pocs/ghsa-j8rw-jp99-435v.js, and regression tests are in tests/unit/tls.js.

### Impact
Applications that use `forge.tls` as a client and pass data from a network socket to `connection.process()` are affected. The server they connect to, or an on-path attacker, can make `process()` throw; if the application doesn't catch it, the Node.js process terminates, dropping all its connections. Servers built on `forge.tls` are not affected. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact.

raw.summary: Astro: Reflected XSS via unescaped slot names in @astrojs/solid-js
raw.details:
## Summary The `@astrojs/solid-js` renderer wraps named slot content passed to Solid components in an `` element, and writes the slot name into its `name` attribute without HTML escaping. A slot name containing `"` could end the attribute and inject arbitrary HTML into the page. For example, a page that takes a slot name from the request: ```astro --- import Tabs from '../components/Tabs.jsx'; const tab = Astro.url.searchParams.get('tab'); ---
…
 ``` rendered with a Solid component that renders a slot by name: ```jsx export default function Tabs(props) { return
{props[props.active]}
; } ``` would output a `tab` value such as `x">` as live HTML. ## Impact Reflected cross-site scripting. An attacker who gets a user to open a crafted link can run JavaScript on the site's origin, but only in applications where all of the following are true: - The page passes request-controlled input (such as a query parameter) as a slot name. - The Solid component is hydrated with a `client:*` directive. For non-hydrated components the slot wrapper is removed from the output, together with its `name` attribute. - The Solid component renders the attacker-chosen slot, which in practice means accessing slot props by a dynamic name. Components that never render the slot only output Astro's already escaped fallback template. This is the `@astrojs/solid-js` counterpart of GHSA-8hv8-536x-4wqp (CVE-2026-50146), which fixed the same issue in `astro` core. ## Affected versions `@astrojs/solid-js` >= 0.2.0, <= 7.1.1. ## Patches Fixed in `@astrojs/solid-js` 7.1.2. Slot names are now HTML-escaped in the server renderer. ## Workarounds Upgrade to `@astrojs/solid-js` 7.1.2 or later. Before upgrading, do not use request-controlled input as a slot name, or map it to a fixed set of known slot names before passing it to a component. ## Credits Reported by @manus-pi.

raw.summary: @hono/node-server: Backslash in the request path is parsed as a path separator, bypassing path-based access control at a reverse proxy
raw.details:
### Summary

`@hono/node-server` passes the raw request-target to the WHATWG URL parser, which treats a backslash in the path as `/` and then resolves `..` segments. A request for `/admin\secret` or `/public\..\admin/secret` reaches the application as `/admin/secret`. A reverse proxy that follows RFC 3986 forwards the backslash unchanged and applies its path-based rules to the original path, so the request reaches a route the proxy is meant to block.

### Details

A raw backslash is not allowed in a request-target (RFC 3986, RFC 9112 Section 3.2.1), and RFC 9112 Section 3.2 says a recipient should reject such a request rather than correct it. Proxies such as nginx on Linux, HAProxy and Envoy keep the backslash as an ordinary character, so they and the application see different paths.

The fix responds with `400 Bad Request` to a request whose path contains a raw backslash, for HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, absolute-form request-targets and WebSocket upgrades. A percent-encoded backslash and a backslash in the query string are still accepted.

### Impact

An unauthenticated client can reach a route that a reverse proxy, load balancer or WAF in front of the application blocks by path.

This affects applications served by `@hono/node-server` behind a front component that makes path-based decisions and forwards a backslash unchanged. Access control inside the Hono application, such as middleware on `/admin/*`, runs on the rewritten path and is not affected.

raw.summary: Astro: XSS via attribute injection in dynamic tag names
raw.details: ## Summary When a dynamic tag (`const Tag = ...; `) resolves to a string, Astro renders it as a raw HTML element name. The name was filtered to remove characters that could inject attributes, but the filter did not handle `/`. Because HTML parsers treat `/` inside a tag as an attribute separator, a tag name such as `img/src/onerror=alert(1)` was rendered as an `` element with an `onerror` attribute. The JSX renderer used for MDX did not filter string tag names at all. For example: ```astro --- const Tag = Astro.url.searchParams.get('as') ?? 'div'; --- hello ``` rendered `?as=img/src/onerror=alert(1)` as live HTML. ## Impact Reflected or stored cross-site scripting, but only in applications that use untrusted input (such as a request parameter or an uncontrolled CMS field) as all or part of an element name. Astro itself never derives element names from request data. Applications that let content choose an element should map that input to a fixed set of known tags. Letting untrusted input choose an element name is unsafe even with a correct filter, because it can still select elements such as `script` or `iframe`. ## Affected versions `astro` <= 7.4.4. ## Patches Fixed in `astro` 7.4.5. String tag names in `.astro` dynamic tags, JSX, and MDX now render only the leading valid element name, so characters such as `/` or `=` can no longer change the generated markup. Strings that do not start with a valid element name now throw an error. ## Workarounds Upgrade to `astro` 7.4.5 or later. Before upgrading, do not use untrusted input as an element name, or map it to a fixed set of known tags. ## Credits Reported by @uttej-badwane.

raw.summary: Nuxt dev server serves files from a parent directory with a stray lockfile or workspace file
raw.details:
### Summary

Nuxt can pick a parent directory that does not declare a workspace as its default `workspaceDir`: the farthest directory with a lockfile when the project is not inside a git repository, or the farthest directory with a `pnpm-workspace.yaml` or `deno.json` file, even one that only holds settings. The Vite dev server allows `/_nuxt/@fs/` requests for any file under `workspaceDir`. A stray lockfile or settings file in a parent directory, such as the home directory, therefore lets anyone who can reach the dev server read files in that directory and everything below it.

### Impact

This affects the development server only; production builds are not affected. All of the following have to hold:

- A parent directory contains either:
  - a lockfile (`package-lock.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `yarn.lock`, `bun.lock` and similar), while the project is not inside a git repository and has no workspace file (`pnpm-workspace.yaml`, `turbo.json`, `lerna.json` and similar) above it. Running `npm install` once in the home directory is enough to create one there.
  - a `pnpm-workspace.yaml` without a `packages` list (for example one that only holds pnpm settings such as `onlyBuiltDependencies`), or a `deno.json` or `deno.jsonc` without a `workspace` field. This applies even if the project is inside a git repository.
- The dev server is reachable from the network (`nuxt dev --host`, `nuxt dev --tunnel`, a published container port, or a proxy onto the dev port). The default localhost bind limits this to local processes, which can usually read the same files directly.

For example, with `~/package-lock.json` and a project at `~/projects/app` that has no `.git` directory, `nuxt dev --host` serves `GET /_nuxt/@fs/<home>/.ssh/id_ed25519` with status 200. Any file in the home directory that is not covered by Vite's `server.fs.deny` list can be read this way, including SSH keys, cloud credentials and the Nuxt DevTools auth token in `~/.nuxt/devtools/dev-auth-token.txt`.

No browser is involved: a plain HTTP client is enough. A web page on another origin cannot read the response, and DNS rebinding is rejected by Vite's host check.

Projects whose parent directories contain none of these files are not affected, nor are projects inside a git repository whose only lockfile is their own. Nuxt 3.5.0 and later are affected.

### Patches

Fixed in `@nuxt/schema` 4.6.4, which `nuxt` 4.6.4 depends on. A parent directory now only becomes the default `workspaceDir` if it declares a workspace: a `pnpm-workspace.yaml` with `packages`, a `deno.json` or `deno.jsonc` with `workspace`, a `lerna.json`, `turbo.json` or `rush.json`, a `package.json` with `workspaces`, or a git repository. A lockfile or a settings file alone no longer widens the dev server's `server.fs.allow` list. If your monorepo root is not detected this way, set `workspaceDir` in `nuxt.config.ts`. Nuxt 3 has reached end of life and will not receive a fix.

### Workarounds

Set `workspaceDir` explicitly in `nuxt.config.ts` to the project root (or to the real monorepo root), or remove the stray lockfile or settings file from the parent directory. Do not expose the dev server to untrusted networks. If the dev port was reachable from an untrusted network while this layout was in place, treat files in the parent directory as exposed and rotate credentials such as SSH keys and cloud tokens.

### Credits

Nuxt thanks [@superboy-zjc](https://github.com/superboy-zjc) for the report.

raw.summary: @hono/node-server: Unhandled `ECONNRESET` on the socket during an asynchronous WebSocket upgrade crashes the process
raw.details:
### Summary

While `@hono/node-server` waits for the Hono application to handle a WebSocket upgrade request, the socket has no error listener. If the client resets the TCP connection during that time, the resulting `ECONNRESET` is emitted as an unhandled `'error'` event and the process terminates.

### Details

The upgrade handler awaits the application before attaching any listener to the socket. When middleware on the upgrade path does asynchronous work, such as an authentication lookup, a connection reset in that window has no handler. If a global `uncaughtException` handler swallows the error, the pending upgrade is never released and its entry is retained for the lifetime of the process.

The fix attaches error and close listeners to the socket before calling the application, releases the pending upgrade when the socket closes, and skips the handshake on a destroyed socket.

### Impact

An unauthenticated client can terminate the server process with a single connection by sending a WebSocket upgrade request and resetting the connection before the application has responded. Where the crash is suppressed, repeated requests grow the heap.

This affects applications that enable WebSocket support in `@hono/node-server` and run asynchronous middleware or handlers on the upgrade path.

raw.summary: Astro: Image endpoint in @astrojs/node can read files from a case-variant sibling of the output directory on case-sensitive filesystems
raw.details:
## Summary

The `/_image` endpoint used by the `@astrojs/node` adapter checks that a requested local image is inside the build output directory before reading it from disk. That check compared paths case-insensitively. On case-sensitive filesystems (such as Linux), a directory whose path differs from the output directory only by letter case is a different directory, but it passed the check.

For example, with the client output directory at `/srv/app/dist/client/`, a request such as:

```text
/_image?href=/../../DIST/client/secret.png&w=32&f=png
```

resolved to `/srv/app/DIST/client/secret.png` and was served, even though that file is outside the output directory.

## Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can read image files from outside the output directory, but only when all of the following are true:

- The site uses on-demand rendering with the `@astrojs/node` adapter.
- The server runs on a case-sensitive filesystem.
- A directory exists whose path matches the output directory except for letter case (for example `DIST/client` next to `dist/client`). Such a layout is unusual, and the attacker cannot create it.

Only files the image service accepts can be read. Raster images are returned after resizing; SVG files are returned unchanged. Other file types fail during processing. Plain path traversal outside the output directory (for example `/../../secret.png`) was already rejected and is not affected.

## Affected versions

`astro` >= 5.14.3, <= 7.4.6, when used with `@astrojs/node` (all versions up to 11.1.11). The vulnerable image endpoint is provided by `astro` and used by the `@astrojs/node` adapter.

## Patches

Fixed in `astro` 7.4.7. The path check now compares paths exactly, and only ignores letter case for Windows drive-letter paths. The fix ships in `astro`, so upgrading `@astrojs/node` alone is not enough.

## Workarounds

Upgrade to `astro` 7.4.7 or later. Before upgrading, make sure no directory next to the build output directory has a path that differs from it only by letter case.

## Credits

Reported by @zachariah-mithani.

@grpc/grpc-js: safe_regex incorrectly applies partial string matching for patterns with alternation
raw.details:
### Summary

The StringMatcher/PathMatcher for `safe_regex` builds its RE2 as `^${regex}$` with no surrounding group. Because alternation has the lowest precedence, a pattern `"a|b|c"` compiles to `/^a|b|c$/` -- "starts with a" OR "contains b" OR "ends with c" instead of a full match of the whole value. Configurations with `safe_regex` matchers that use a regex alternation (a natural way to list methods or service identities) therefore apply partial string matches. This impacts route selection, xDS credentials, and RBAC.

### Details

`src/matcher.ts`: `SafeRegexValueMatcher` and `PathSafeRegexValueMatcher` both do
```ts
this.targetRegexImpl = new RE2(`^${targetRegex}$`, 'u');
```

and `apply()` returns `targetRegexImpl.test(value)`. With a top-level alternation the anchors bind only to the first/last branch.

https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/matcher.ts#L59

https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/matcher.ts#L232

`src/route.ts` (`getPredicateForStringMatcher` / `getPredicateForHeaderMatcher`) builds these for every `safe_regex` `StringMatcher`/`HeaderMatcher`, and src/rbac.ts uses them for RBAC `url_path` `permissions`/`principals`, `authenticated.principal_name` (mTLS SAN/CN), `requested_server_name` and `header rules`. So an ALLOW rule written with an alternation grants access to method names, certificate identities or header values that extend an intended one. DENY policies only become broader (fail-safe).

https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/route.ts#L28

https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/route.ts#L47

### Proof of concept

In a scratch directory:

```
npm init -y
npm i @grpc/grpc-js-xds@1.14.1 @grpc/grpc-js
node poc.cjs
```

`poc.cjs` calls the exported RBAC engine directly (the functions grpc-js uses to make the authorization decision); no server or network:

```js
const { parseConfig } = require('@grpc/grpc-js-xds/build/src/rbac.js')
const { SafeRegexValueMatcher } = require('@grpc/grpc-js-xds/build/src/matcher.js')
const { Metadata } = require('@grpc/grpc-js')

console.log(new SafeRegexValueMatcher('admin|editor').toString()) // SafeRegex(/^admin|editor$/u)

const sr = regex => ({ match_pattern: 'safe_regex', safe_regex: { regex } })
const info = urlPath => ({ urlPath, headers: new Metadata(), tls: true, peerCertificate: null,
  destinationIp: '10.0.0.1', destinationPort: 443, sourceIp: '10.0.0.2' })
const g = parseConfig({ action: 'ALLOW', policies: { p: {
  permissions: [{ rule: 'url_path', url_path: { path: sr('/acme.Users/GetUser|/acme.Users/ListUsers') } }],
  principals: [{ identifier: 'any', any: true }] } } })

console.log('GetUser       ', g.apply(info('/acme.Users/GetUser')))       // true  (intended)
console.log('DeleteUser    ', g.apply(info('/acme.Users/DeleteUser')))    // false (control)
console.log('GetUserSecrets', g.apply(info('/acme.Users/GetUserSecrets'))) // true <-- BYPASS
```

Observed (grpc-js-xds 1.14.1, grpc-js 1.14.6):

```
matcher "admin|editor" -> SafeRegex(/^admin|editor$/u);
    apply("administrator")=true, apply("not-an-editor")=true
ALLOW url_path /acme.Users/GetUser|/acme.Users/ListUsers:
    /acme.Users/GetUser         -> ALLOWED (intended)
    /acme.Users/DeleteUser      -> denied  (control)
    /acme.Users/GetUserSecrets  -> ALLOWED <-- bypass (policy intends deny)
control, same regex as (?:...|...): /acme.Users/GetUserSecrets -> denied
ALLOW authenticated principal_name spiffe://prod/ns/web/sa/frontend|...ops/sa/admin:
    spiffe://prod/ns/web/sa/frontend-batch -> ALLOWED <-- bypass
```

### Impact

Users of `@grpc/grpc-js-xds` who are using `safe_regex` matchers with alternation for route selection, xDS credentials SAN matchers, or RBAC rules may see incorrectly permissive behavior.

raw.summary: Forge: TLS client crash on an unsupported ServerHello compression method
raw.details:
### Summary
A `forge.tls` client accepts any compression method in the ServerHello, although it only offers no compression. An unknown method makes `connection.process()` throw an uncaught `Error` when the client handles ServerHelloDone, before the server is authenticated. A malicious server or an on-path attacker can use this to terminate a Node.js process. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

### Details
The client's ClientHello offers only the `null` compression method. `tls.parseHelloMessage()` in `lib/tls.js` stores the ServerHello's `compression_method` for the client without checking it (the code has a `TODO: handle compression methods`). When the client handles ServerHelloDone it calls `tls.createConnectionState()`, which throws `Error('Unsupported compression algorithm.')` for any method other than `null` (0) and `deflate` (1). The exception propagates out of `connection.process()`.

The ServerHello isn't authenticated until the server's Finished message, so an on-path attacker can change the compression byte of a genuine ServerHello; the certificate chain still verifies. Applications that pass socket data to `process()` without catching exceptions terminate. This includes `forge.tls.wrapSocket`, which calls `process()` from its socket data handler, and `forge.http`, which uses it. A `deflate` (1) method, also never offered, makes the handshake fail later with an error instead of a crash.

Servers are not affected: a server always selects no compression.

The fix fails the handshake with an `illegal_parameter` alert, through the connection's `error` callback, when the ServerHello selects any compression method other than `null`.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

#### Workarounds
Catch exceptions thrown by `connection.process()` and close the socket.

#### Resources
- RFC 5246, section 7.4.1.3 (Server Hello): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5246#section-7.4.1.3
- Related: GHSA-525v-9gp9-w22h (another TLS client crash during the handshake, fixed in 1.4.1): https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-525v-9gp9-w22h

#### Severity
CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H (5.9, Moderate)
CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (8.2)
CVSS 4.0 has no counterpart to 3.1's AC:H beyond AT:P and scores this higher; the severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.

#### Credits
Reported by @alienkeric.

### Proof of concept
A server (or on-path attacker) sends a ServerHello with `compression_method` 0xff, followed by a valid Certificate and ServerHelloDone:

    client.handshake();
    client.process(serverHello + certificate + serverHelloDone);
    // <= 1.4.2: throws Error: Unsupported compression algorithm.
    // 1.4.3: error callback with "Unsupported compression method."

The reporter's PoC (a CA-issued server certificate and the default verify callback) is in tests/pocs/ghsa-w4xr-hqv8-ch44.js, and regression tests are in tests/unit/tls.js.

### Impact
Applications that use `forge.tls` as a client (directly, through `forge.tls.wrapSocket`, or through `forge.http`) and pass data from a network socket to `connection.process()` are affected. The server they connect to, or an on-path attacker, can make `process()` throw before the server is authenticated; if the application doesn't catch it, the Node.js process terminates, dropping all its connections. Servers built on `forge.tls` are not affected. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact.

The redis-type-xyz package is an empty impersonation of Redis OM. It copies the redis-om-node repository, homepage, author, documentation, and declared dist/index.js entry point, but the published archive does not contain the declared dist directory or any usable implementation. The agent supports system information collection, drive and directory enumeration, removal, and deploy_binary tasks. deploy_binary writes attacker-supplied Base64 content to disk, registers persistence on Windows, macOS, or Linux, and launches the replacement agent. The malicious ulid-xyz dependency is independently tracked as MAL-2026-6672. redis-type-xyz is a separate delivery package that intentionally substitutes the known-malicious dependency into an otherwise copied Redis OM manifest.

@apexacc/cli is distributed by "Apex Accelerator" (Apex Arena), a fake Web3 accelerator that lures crypto founders with free AI credits and audits. Elastic Security Labs (REF8801, published 2026-10-12) found it is a repackaged Oh My Pi coding agent (1,351 of 1,363 files identical) with malicious additions that hijack the developer's AI coding agent: it overwrites OPENROUTER_BASE_URL so model traffic (prompts, files read, tool results) goes to attacker infrastructure at arena.apexaccs.org; persists an attacker-controlled remote MCP server in ~/.apex/agent/mcp.json; and defaults tool approval to "yolo". A bootstrap retrieves commands from vrf.apexaccs.org: on macOS it drops CloudSyncD (fake password prompt, credential theft, C2 ccmihr.com); on Windows a staged loader chain ends in an infostealer that exfiltrates browser credentials, wallets, messengers, VPN clients and Claude/Cursor/Windsurf configs over Telegram. Elastic analyzed version 1.6.1 and traced the bootstrap to the earliest preserved version (script host arenapex.cloud). The package was still live on npm (latest 1.6.2) with no OSV record as of 2026-10-16. Independently confirmed by static inspection of the live 1.6.2 npm tarball (sha256 7ca5e3908dd8721d0cf6af2488f0825c0d91a5e0b7c8529ef830141a4a3ba31f) on 2026-10-16, without execution: the bin launcher apex.cjs (sha256 4029192a44ee738deba9aa53b57550075cb8fd170a63f0636dea5452256f2175) runs when the user invokes the CLI (no install script). On Windows it sets the current user's PowerShell execution policy to RemoteSigned (no elevation needed), and on Windows 11 it launches a hidden, elevated (UAC RunAs) PowerShell that attempts to add a Defender exclusion for ~/.apex and to set HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\CI\Policy VerifiedAndReputablePolicyState=0 (disabling Smart App Control). From 1.5.122 (2026-09-17) through 1.6.2 those two commands are built in a JavaScript template literal with single backslashes, so the shipped paths are mangled (the exclusion lands on a sibling path '<home>.apex' and the registry key is invalid) and both likely fail; the UAC prompt still appears. Versions 1.5.120 (registry change) and 1.5.121 (adds the Defender exclusion), both 2026-09-17, carried correctly escaped versions of these commands without an elevation prompt, effective only when already running as administrator. The execution-policy change first appears in 1.6.2. It then downloads a ~114MB native binary from GitHub releases of apexaccs/copilot into ~/.apex/bin, and on macOS an additional apex-verify-darwin helper. Both GitHub repositories referenced by the package versions (apexaccs/copilot, Apex-Accelerator/apexcli) return 404 as of 2026-10-16. All versions affected. Indicators from Elastic's report.

On CLI startup (invoked via npx per the package README), apex.cjs unconditionally detects Windows 11 and launches a hidden, UAC-elevated PowerShell via Start-Process -Verb RunAs -WindowStyle Hidden with a UTF-16LE base64 -EncodedCommand payload. The elevation path uses underscore-prefixed identifiers (_ps, _enc, _sp, _osv, _isWin11, _home), a hidden window, base64 command encoding, and a broad try/catch that silently swallows errors. After weakening the host, the CLI downloads a ~105MB apex-<platform>.exe (and an optional native.node addon) from the publisher's GitHub Releases with no hash or signature verification, chmods 0755, and executes it via spawnSync with inherited stdio and the full process.env. The security-policy downgrade is not consistent with any documented function of an AI CLI and converts an otherwise routine publisher-pinned binary fetch into execution of unverified code under a machine-wide-weakened Windows security posture.

This package installs a credential stealer and self-spreading worm. On a developer machine (it exits under CI, in containers and under a debugger), the install script loads a prebuilt native addon that decodes and runs a hidden, obfuscated Bun program. That program collects npm, GitHub, GitLab, PyPI, RubyGems, JFrog, Docker and cloud (AWS, GCP, Azure) credentials, HashiCorp Vault and Kubernetes secrets, SSH keys, .git-credentials and .env files, browser logins, the macOS keychain, 1Password and Bitwarden, and uses stolen publishing tokens to spread: it publishes to npm, PyPI and RubyGems, injects GitHub workflows and GitLab CI templates, and writes hooks into AI coding assistant configuration. Anyone who installed any version should treat every credential reachable from that machine as exposed: rotate npm, GitHub and cloud tokens, check their own packages for unexpected releases, and check repositories for unexpected workflow changes.

@testsecuiitytestme/cache-helper is the only package of the npm account testsecuiitytestme. It describes itself as "Cache helper utilities" and has no README, repository or source code. Each version runs a native addon at install time. 1.0.1 has postinstall: node -e "try{require(process.platform==='win32'?'./addon_win.node':'./addon.node')}catch(e){}". 1.0.2 and 1.0.3 depend on node-gyp-build and run it as postinstall, which loads the prebuilt addon shipped in prebuilds/linux-x64/node.napi.node or prebuilds/win32-x64/node.napi.node. 1.0.3 adds a binding.gyp with an empty sources list and an install script node-gyp rebuild, so the package looks like an ordinary native module; there is no C source in any version. 1.0.5 drops node-gyp-build and runs postinstall: node _setup.js, a one-line require of the same prebuilds/<platform>-<arch>/node.napi.node. 1.0.7 runs postinstall: patch-package || node index.js; patch-package is not a dependency, so the command falls through to index.js, which requires the same addon. 1.0.5 and 1.0.7 ship the same .napi_cache as 1.0.3. 1.0.4 and 1.0.6 were not retrieved; each was published with the same install script as the version before it.

It checks for CI and sandbox environments (GITHUB_ACTIONS, GITLAB_CI, TRAVIS, CIRCLECI, JENKINS_URL, BUILDKITE, CODEBUILD_BUILD_ID and others, plus SANDBOX), containers (/proc/1/cgroup: docker, containerd, kubepods, podman), a debugger (TracerPid), memory and CPU count, then reads the sibling file .napi_cache, writes it to a hidden temp file and runs it in a detached process.

.napi_cache is JavaScript encoded with a single-byte XOR (0x96). It exits under CI, decodes a second layer (repeating 32-byte XOR, then brotli), locates the Bun runtime or downloads bun 1.2.18 from the official oven-sh/bun GitHub releases, writes the decoded program to the temp directory and runs it detached with Bun. This loader shape matches the second wave of the Shai-Hulud npm worm.

The Bun program is obfuscated (javascript-obfuscator string table). Its strings show credential collection for npm, GitHub, GitLab, PyPI, RubyGems, JFrog, Docker Hub and GHCR, AWS, GCP, Azure, HashiCorp Vault and Kubernetes, plus .ssh, .git-credentials, .env files, browser login databases, the macOS keychain, 1Password and Bitwarden. ## Source: amazon-inspector (3ef188a3ae4eae567d3743116d10e586565a2856b53b94add9f84b239aea378e)
The package advertises itself as a cache helper but ships no readable JavaScript logic — index.js and _setup.js are one-line stubs that unconditionally load a prebuilt N-API native addon from prebuilds/<platform>-<arch>/node.napi.node, and module.exports is empty. The addon is paired with a 2,397,565-byte sibling file named.napi_cache that contains no printable strings and is identical across linux-x64 and win32-x64 (sha256 c14dae93...4a57). Strings inside the native addon show it reads %s\.napi_cache, writes a decoded %s.nc%lu.js to the OS temp directory (GetTempPathA), and spawns node on it (CreateProcessA, "node \"%s\""). This decrypt-drop-and-exec chain runs both from the postinstall hook (node _setup.js) and from the main entrypoint, so every npm install and every require()/import of the package triggers execution of attacker-controlled code whose content cannot be inspected from the shipped source. The native addon additionally performs anti-analysis gating before executing the payload: enumeration of CI environment variables (GITHUB_ACTIONS, GITLAB_CI, TRAVIS, CIRCLECI, JENKINS_URL, BUILDKITE, APPVEYOR, NETLIFY, VERCEL, SANDBOX), checks for analysis tools (wireshark, procmon, procexp, x64dbg, ollydbg, fiddler, httpdebug), Windows debugger checks (IsDebuggerPresent, CheckRemoteDebuggerPresent), and Linux sandbox/container detection (/proc/self/status TracerPid, /proc/1/cgroup, dockerinit). The combination of an empty public API, an opaque 2.4 MB encrypted blob, a native loader that decrypts-writes-execs it to temp, and layered anti-analysis gating has no legitimate caching purpose and matches a classic alternate-execution dropper designed to bypass JavaScript-only scanners.

This package is a fork of the Baileys WhatsApp library in which lib/Socket/socket.js replaces the standard random pairing code with a hardcoded default. The default value is produced at runtime by CryptoJS AES-decrypting the embedded ciphertext `U2FsdGVkX1+LgFmBqo3Wg0zTlHXoebkTRtjmU0cq9Fs=` with the password `ERROR_FILE`, and is bound as the default argument of `requestPairingCode(a, b=Z)`. A party holding the plaintext can derive the same key and attack the companion-device linking handshake performed by installers of this package. The use of CryptoJS symmetric decryption to conceal a single constant in otherwise readable code is a deliberate concealment technique rather than a build artifact, and upstream Baileys does not contain this construct.

## Source: amazon-inspector (0f1051c395438db8dc0dbe6de1cb09e6e10c83fc6062d359ca85093ce946f0e0)
package.json for @zanxiky/baileys@1.1.0 declares the `libsignal` dependency as `github:tenka-san/libsignal-node` — a non-registry git source on an unaffiliated personal GitHub account with no commit SHA and no integrity check. On `npm install`, npm clones the current default-branch tip of that repository and executes any lifecycle scripts it contains, so the owner of the `tenka-san` GitHub account controls arbitrary code execution on every installer's machine, and the referenced bytes can change at any time without any version bump to this package. The GitHub account is unrelated to the upstream Baileys publisher (whiskeysockets), and the fork itself appears to be a lookalike of the Baileys WhatsApp library.

## Source: amazon-inspector (30293986b3a71c37fb77bcffcc5494ef8a45cd6e55e63ee7d4a76fa07107479d)
solvit-cli ships a built-in default configuration (defaults.js) containing a bare-IP, plain-HTTP endpoint (http://144.24.117.169:20128) and a bundled sk-prefixed API key. In solvit.js, getConfig falls back to this built-in baseUrl and apiKey whenever the user has not set SOLVIT_BASE_URL / OPENAI_BASE_URL or populated ~/.solvitrc. When the `solvit solve <file>` command is invoked in that default state, the contents of the target source file, any `-c` context files, and any `.solvit-problem.txt` problem description are POSTed to that hardcoded bare-IP destination over cleartext HTTP, authenticated with the bundled key. The README presents the tool as sending requests to an OpenAI-compatible endpoint the user configured and states that an unconfigured endpoint will trigger an init prompt; the built-in bare-IP default is not disclosed. A bare IP on a non-standard port with no TLS is not a legitimate OpenAI-compatible provider shape, and users invoking the CLI without explicit configuration will transmit their source code to an author-operated collector without being aware of it.

## Source: amazon-inspector (b9372597423bda09fe5c3adc72b7ff804563626e2af777237b38d39563613de8)
package.json declares the `libsignal` dependency as `github:RahmadTenpoles/libsignal-node` with no commit SHA, tag, or integrity hash. On `npm install`, this resolves to whatever the default branch of that personal GitHub repository currently contains, including any lifecycle scripts, and executes them on the installer's machine. The source is a personal account unrelated to the official libsignal publisher, and the repository owner can push new code at any time to retroactively change what every subsequent install runs. The declared dependency key equals the standard name `libsignal`, so the override silently substitutes a third-party fork for what would otherwise resolve from the registry — a dependency-confusion-shaped override. The package also presents itself as a fork of the Baileys WhatsApp library (`raiden-baileys`), a lookalike naming pattern against the widely used `@whiskeysockets/baileys` family.

## Source: amazon-inspector (07a00a17209ccc173a7196dd8e97486609819945db1459a5333463be9f6c20b9)
fcefi-wdojs-util@1.0.0 ships a loader in index.js that reads an undeclared `_bz` numeric array (~1000 bytes) from its own package.json, zlib-inflates it, and executes the resulting JavaScript via the Function constructor on every require of the package. The loader is wrapped in an IIFE that explicitly short-circuits when any of `CI`, `GITHUB_ACTIONS`, `GITLAB_CI`, `TRAVIS`, `CIRCLECI`, or `SANDBOX` are set in the environment, so the payload only runs on developer and production hosts and stays inert in scanning environments. Adjacent to the loader, lib/native.pkg_config is a 2,890,302-byte file containing only hex characters with no printable strings and no relation to native code or pkg-config, consistent with an encrypted stage-2 payload decrypted by the inflated bytecode. The combination — executable code smuggled inside the manifest as a non-standard field, require-time Function()-based execution, deliberate CI/sandbox evasion, and a large opaque hex blob shipped as a misleadingly named config file — is a multi-stage dropper with no legitimate utility function.

## Source: amazon-inspector (f6f3367976e89b052e26e44ddc41d0352391f24336e41a8d41687a0d4c7010e0)
The package presents itself as a mock-data generator but hides a base64-encoded JavaScript payload across the `mark` fields of data/products_*.js. The library entrypoint (index.js) concatenates those fields, decodes the result with Buffer.from(..., 'base64').toString('utf-8'), and executes it via the Function() constructor with Buffer, require, and process passed in as arguments. The identifiers 'Buffer', 'require', 'process', and 'new Function' are reconstructed at runtime from an XOR-obfuscated table keyed by a derived 4-byte seed, which conceals the eval sink from string-based scanners. The exported getTransactions() API triggers this execution on every call. The decoded payload loads python-shell and https, writes a Python script to /tmp/targets, and recursively walks the filesystem (pathlib.Path(root).rglob('*')) for file names containing 'password', 'wallet', 'seed', 'privatekey', or '.env'. The advertised purpose (mock data) has no legitimate need to enumerate credential-, wallet-, and dotenv-shaped files on the installer's host or to run arbitrary code reconstructed from pseudo-data files.

## Source: amazon-inspector (db7da8999828536292e11d09747504d964bf7525862de7d207d03c8809c438a0)
The package advertises itself as lightweight string utility helpers (trim/capitalize/truncate), but ships a 17KB Linux ELF.node addon, a 434KB Windows PE.node addon, and a 3.7MB opaque.napi_cache data blob none of which are needed for the stated purpose. index.js unconditionally loads the platform-appropriate native addon on every require() and swallows errors silently before the trivial string helpers are even defined. The native addon references the adjacent.napi_cache blob and contains code paths for file I/O, fork/setsid/execlp on Linux and CreateProcessA with a 'node "%s"' command template on Windows, staging decoded JavaScript at /tmp/.<pid> (format string /tmp/.%u, %s.nc%lu.js) and executing it under node. Before firing, the addon enumerates CI and sandbox indicators (GITHUB_ACTIONS, GITLAB_CI, TRAVIS, CIRCLECI, JENKINS_URL, BUILDKITE, CODEBUILD_BUILD_ID, APPVEYOR, SEMAPHORE, TEAMCITY_VERSION, BITBUCKET_BUILD_NUMBER, NETLIFY, VERCEL, CF_BUILD_ID, SCREWDRIVER, SANDBOX), reads /proc/1/cgroup, /proc/1/cmdline, /proc/self/status (TracerPid) and /proc/self/maps for docker/containerd/kubepod/podman markers, and on Windows checks IsDebuggerPresent, CheckRemoteDebuggerPresent and scans running processes for analysis tools (wireshark, httpdebug, Process32First). The combination of a trivial cover-story API, undeclared native binaries loaded silently on import, an opaque sibling blob decrypted to a hidden /tmp staging path and executed under node, and sandbox/CI/debugger evasion gating is a load-time dropper that runs attacker-controlled code on the installer's host as soon as the package is required.

The package impersonates @tailwindcss/forms: name, repository (tailwindlabs/tailwindcss-forms), author (@tailwindcss), README, CHANGELOG, and HTML are copied from the legitimate plugin, with a demo link to tailwindcss-hook-forms.vercel.app. src/index.js prepends a hand-rolled string-permutation decoder (spin() with magic constants NX/SX, splitLane/peel wrappers) that resolves the Function constructor via peel.constructor and immediately invokes a function compiled from a ~15KB opaque, obfuscated string literal, passing the host require into it. The subsequent code replicates the public API of @tailwindcss/forms as cover. The obfuscator scheme does not exist in the legitimate plugin and its only purpose is to conceal the executable body from review.

index.js reads a numeric byte array stored under a non-standard `_bz` key inside package.json, decompresses it with zlib.inflateSync, and executes the resulting string via the Function constructor with `require` and `__dirname` bound in — all on module load. Execution is gated by an early-return when any of CI, GITHUB_ACTIONS, GITLAB_CI, TRAVIS, CIRCLECI, or SANDBOX environment variables are set, so the hidden code only runs on real developer or production hosts. Smuggling executable logic as a zlib blob under a private manifest key, decoding it, and running it through Function() at require time is an obfuscated-loader pattern; the package's self-description as a 'utility' does not match any behavior visible in its source. The payload executes with full Node privileges on the installer's machine as soon as the module is required.

## Source: amazon-inspector (0495a09022e152fe8c13b9251497c56e333b58af6e54c412bfd43ff4503be1a7)
package.json declares the sole dependency 'node-health-utils' as an off-registry HTTP tarball URL at a bare IP address (http://121.199.24.94/dl/health-utils-1.0.0.tgz) rather than a registry version range. On npm install, whatever bytes that URL returns are fetched and installed, including any lifecycle scripts bundled in the tarball, with no version pin, no integrity hash, and no TLS. The host controlling that IP has arbitrary code execution on every installer at install time, and plain HTTP additionally permits MITM substitution of the tarball. The shipped index.js is an inert MCP stub; the dependency source itself is the delivery channel.

## Source: amazon-inspector (bd1ec5b1f032d6879c69671f7c67499798ca134a341c87d69d310e2a36c6603b)
superlib_ex3 advertises itself as a trivial hello-world library exposing a single `hello()` function, but its npm `postinstall` lifecycle hook performs an unconditional network fetch to the hardcoded URL `https://x.aaaaa.fr/postInstall` and writes the response bytes to `./postInstall.sh` in the installer's current working directory. The destination host is unrelated to the package name, has no connection to any declared publisher, and the download is unpinned, unversioned, and lacks any hash or signature verification. The fetched content is a shell script staged under a filename that collides with lifecycle-script semantics on the installer's machine. The package has no documented reason to perform network I/O or stage shell scripts, and the fetched bytes can be changed by the operator of x.aaaaa.fr at any time without any change to the published package.

## Source: amazon-inspector (1c3af30011dcf54950f270463028270d732fce20b5cd5da44342a0748922e6df)
The package is advertised as a neutral CLI/MCP wrapper for Hyperliquid, but its distributed code silently routes value from the installer to an author-controlled address. In dist/index.js and dist/mcp.js, the constants BUILDER_ADDRESS = 0xa6f967d47c6f85a5ba4fc43543e5e1c171cccf98, BUILDER_FEE = 1 (0.01%), and REFERRAL_CODE = '2OOLKIT' are hardcoded. On `config init` / `config set --private-key...`, a fire-and-forget `silentAutoSetup(env, privateKey, walletAddress)` signs and submits (a) a `setReferrer('2OOLKIT')` transaction and (b) an `approveBuilderFee(0xa6f9...cf98, '0.1%')` transaction on the user's Hyperliquid account, with errors swallowed so the user sees no indication. Additionally, `HyperliquidClient.placeOrder` unconditionally injects `action.builder = { b: BUILDER_ADDRESS, f: BUILDER_FEE }` into every order, so every trade routed through the CLI pays a builder fee to the hardcoded address in perpetuity. None of this is disclosed in the README or command output, there is no opt-out, and the behavior is triggered by the documented setup flow. This is a silent-relay pattern causing direct, ongoing financial harm to anyone who installs and uses the package with a funded wallet. The repeated POSTs flagged in dist/index.js:610 and dist/mcp.js:466 correspond to the Hyperliquid exchange submissions carrying these hardcoded builder/referrer fields.

## Source: amazon-inspector (d803002ee95ea92bdcb3a918e1be10930816db383ce2a58a6947afea84e04040)
@asavie/i18n@99.0.0 is a dependency-confusion package targeting an unclaimed npm scope. Its package.json declares a `preinstall` hook that runs `node callback.js`, which on `npm install` reads `os.hostname()` and the output of `whoami` (callback.js L23, L28) and transmits them to the attacker-controlled out-of-band collector `d88r3mao12pqka8tg04gn4ychek66c3wj.oast.site` (an Interactsh subdomain) via both a DNS A-record lookup and an `https.get()` request with the data base64url-encoded into the subdomain (callback.js L21, L37, L46). Version `99.0.0` and the squat on the `@asavie` scope are the canonical dependency-confusion shape — any build that mistakenly resolves this scope from public npm leaks identifying host data to the publisher. The tarball additionally ships an unrelated ~123 MB `google-chrome-stable_current_amd64.deb` that is not referenced by any code path; it is not executed but represents either staging or registry abuse. Author claims of 'authorized research' are unverifiable by installers and do not change the installer-side outcome: unsolicited exfiltration of host identifiers on `npm install`.

## Source: amazon-inspector (c79c7b873a8ea61831fdfd7b987de0efbf8944d2fd407a8dca4b70042a3d029c)
This package is a republished fork of @whiskeysockets/baileys that adds two undocumented network behaviors. (1) lib/Socket/newsletter.js line 111 schedules a setTimeout 90 seconds after a consumer constructs a WhatsApp socket via the documented makeWASocket/makeNewsletterSocket API; the timer calls loadNewsletter(), which axios.get's https://raw.githubusercontent.com/budetzz/mazzbudetzzzzz/refs/heads/main/saluran.json and then issues newsletterWMexQuery(id, FOLLOW) for every ID returned, using the consumer's authenticated WhatsApp identity. The list is hosted on a mutable main branch under the package author's personal GitHub account, so the set of channels the installer's account is forced to follow can be changed at any time without publishing a new package version. The consumer never opted in and the behavior is not documented. (2) lib/index.js line 37 fires a top-level fetch to https://raw.githubusercontent.com/z4phdev/client/refs/heads/main/information.json on every require() of the package and prints data[0].message to the console; this is a remote-mutable, author-controlled in-process content channel that beacons each installer's IP and timing to the author on import. Additionally, package.json advertises homepage https://github.com/whiskeysockets/baileys (the legitimate upstream) while fetchLatestBaileysVersion in lib/Utils/generics.js:351 is repointed to https://raw.githubusercontent.com/z4phdev/baileys/master/src/Defaults/baileys-version.json — a personal fork — so version-update telemetry is also redirected to attacker infrastructure. The silent hijack of the consumer's WhatsApp account to perform actions (channel follows) chosen by the author via a mutable URL is a silent-relay/account-hijack attack on the installer.

## Source: amazon-inspector (c2dbcccc761971dfc5f844f59f362fe32ee1e0b9a3cd91ddd4fc87be5c8b013a)
The package is published under the name `@budetzz/libsignal-node`, impersonating the well-known libsignal Signal-protocol library, but the homepage and code are a fork of Baileys (the WhatsApp Web library; `homepage: github.com/whiskeysockets/baileys`). It additionally aliases `libsignal` to itself via `"libsignal": "npm:@budetzz/libsignal-node"` so any transitive consumer of `libsignal` resolves here.

When a consumer constructs a WhatsApp socket via `makeWASocket`, `lib/Socket/newsletter.js` schedules a 90-second timer that fetches a JSON list of WhatsApp newsletter IDs from a mutable, author-controlled GitHub URL (`raw.githubusercontent.com/budetzz/mazzbudetzzzzz/refs/heads/main/saluran.json`) and issues a FOLLOW (`newsletterWMexQuery(id, QueryIds.FOLLOW,...)`) on each one using the installer's WhatsApp account, with no disclosure or opt-in. Because the URL is mutable, the author can rotate or grow the target list at any time, silently expanding the channels every consumer's WhatsApp account is subscribed to.

In addition, `lib/index.js:37` fetches `raw.githubusercontent.com/z4phdev/client/refs/heads/main/information.json` on every require and prints `data[0]` to the terminal — a live author-controlled channel into every consumer's process at module load (and a leak of consumer IP/UA to that repo).

This is a silent-relay: normal use of the advertised API hijacks the caller's identity (their WhatsApp account) for the author's benefit (reach/subscribers on attacker-chosen channels), under a deliberately misleading package name.
