  run. The stale-tagtype copy is a Python-side hygiene bug in its own right,
  but its memory-safety consequence exists only because the encoder lets a
  non-tuple value reach `TIFFSetField(COLORMAP)`.

## Impact

Any service that accepts a TIFF and writes it back out as TIFF through libtiff —
which happens with a plain `im.save(fp, "TIFF")` whenever the uploaded file is
compressed, or whenever a `compression=` other than raw is requested — returns
to the uploader, inside one metadata tag of the produced file, an
attacker-chosen number of bytes read from a stale pointer in the worker process,
deterministically and without retries. Which memory that is depends on the
compiler's register allocation for `PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew`: in this clang
build the pointer is `_imaging.so + 0x1588`, so a request for 262 144 bytes
(which succeeded every time in testing, as did 2 000 000) covers the
extension's `.rodata`, `.data.rel.ro`/GOT and `.data` and returned 2 800+
resolved pointers into libpython, libc, libtiff, libjpeg and others — a complete
ASLR bypass for chaining with any other memory bug; a gcc build of the same
source left a different, unrelated address in that slot. The fixed-count
variant kills the worker process with SIGSEGV from a 181-byte upload on every
request. With `tiffinfo=im.tag_v2` the source
address is fully attacker-chosen (16-byte arbitrary read into the output for
ActiveArea, or a crash). No non-default Pillow setting is involved; the only
precondition is TIFF-to-TIFF re-encoding.

The other branches add further deterministic process-kill inputs (BYTE-typed
ColorMap in any RGB or palette TIFF; `thumbnail()` keeps `tag_v2`, so
open→thumbnail→save-as-TIFF is affected too) and extend the reach to
JPEG/PNG/WebP uploads whose EXIF is preserved with `exif=` when converting to
libtiff-compressed TIFF. All the memory errors are reads; libtiff sizes its
destination buffers with the same count it copies, so no out-of-bounds write
was found.

## Reproducing

`repro` is one Python script, run against the stock build with the installed `PIL`. It needs no compiler and no extra files.

`upload(tag, value)` has Pillow write a 16×16 red RGB image as an LZW-compressed TIFF, then appends a new IFD holding the same entries plus one extra `<tag> / LONG / count 1 / value` (kept in tag order) and points the header at it — a 356-byte input on this tree. The source is LZW-compressed on purpose. A bare `im.save(out, "TIFF")` keeps the source's compression, so the save goes through the libtiff writer even though the application passes no arguments. `resave()` is the whole "application": `Image.open(BytesIO(src)); im.save(out, "TIFF")`.

The script runs three cases:

1. **Control, tag 65000 = 4096.** libtiff does not know this tag, so the file is re-saved correctly and the output tag reads back as the integer `4096`. This is what should happen to every tag.
2. **Leak, DNGPrivateData 50740 = 65536.** libtiff's built-in definition of this tag is a counted BYTE array. It reads Pillow's single scalar as the *count* and takes the data pointer from a vararg slot Pillow never wrote. The output tag comes back as `bytes` of length 65536 that do not occur in the input. The script prints the first 32 of them and the file offset at which they occur in `_imaging.so` on disk. On this build they always do (offset `0x57588`): the stale pointer aims into the extension's read-only data.
3. **Wild read, ActiveArea 50829 = 64.** libtiff defines this tag as a fixed LONG[4] array with no count, so it uses the scalar 64 as the *source address*. The script re-runs itself as a child process (`repro child`, core dumps disabled) to do this re-save, and the child exits with `-11`, meaning SIGSEGV.

Expected output on the affected tree:

```
control  tag 65000=4096 -> 4096
leak     tag 50740=65536 from a 356-byte upload -> 65536 bytes not present in input, head a661fcffc661fcff3360fcff7b61fcffd361fcff085ffcffe061fcff3360fcff
         leaked bytes found in _imaging.so at file offset 0x57588
crash    tag 50829=64 -> child exit -11 (SIGSEGV)
BUG
```

The script prints `BUG` if case 2 leaks or case 3 crashes. Both are deterministic on this build. A fixed Pillow prints `OK`: the tag does not come back as 65536 bytes of foreign data (it reads back as `None`, or `save()` raises `ValueError`/`RuntimeError`, which the script catches), and the child exits with something other than SIGSEGV (0, or 1 if `save()` raised).

The other branches can be checked by hand on the stock build in the same way
(each as `Image.open(f); im.save(BytesIO(), "TIFF")` in a child process):
a PackBits RGB TIFF with an extra IFD entry `320 / BYTE / 4 / "ABCD"` →
SIGSEGV every run; a PackBits palette TIFF whose ColorMap is `320 / BYTE / 2`
saved with `tiffinfo=im.tag_v2` → SIGSEGV every run; a Pillow-written JPEG
whose EXIF holds tag 50000 = RATIONAL×2 saved with
`compression="tiff_lzw", exif=im.info["exif"]` → SIGSEGV in most runs,
`RuntimeError` ("Failed to allocate memory for custom tag binary object
(-N elements of 4 bytes each)") in the rest.

## Suggested fix

The encoder must not guess the calling convention; it has to ask libtiff what
the tag's effective definition is *after* `ImagingLibTiffMergeFieldInfo` and
marshal accordingly, or refuse. The attached patch does this for non-core tags:

* a new `ImagingLibTiffFindField()` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` (declared
  in `TiffDecode.h`, next to the other libtiff wrappers) returns libtiff's
  `TIFFFindField` type, `passcount` and `writecount` for a tag;
* in `PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew` (`src/encode.c`), for a non-core tag that
  libtiff already knows, Pillow adopts libtiff's type when it has none of its
  own, and after `ImagingLibTiffMergeFieldInfo` a new `tiff_field_matches()`
  checks the value against libtiff's definition: a scalar only for a
  single-value field whose C argument type (int / `uint64_t` / double /
  `char *`) matches, an array only with libtiff's element size and, for
  fixed-count fields, exactly `writecount` elements. Anything else raises
  `ValueError("Tag value does not match libtiff field definition")` instead of
  reaching `TIFFSetField` — this covers the reproducer's DNGPrivateData and
  ActiveArea inputs, ASCII-typed Photoshop, short PrimaryChromaticities and the
  `LONG8` `tiffinfo=` variant;
* every tuple/`bytes` branch now goes through `set_tiff_array_field()`, which
  passes `len` only when the field has `passcount` set; this also fixes the
  `TIFF_RATIONAL` branch, which never passed a count (and extends it to
  `TIFF_SRATIONAL`);
* `TIFF_UNDEFINED` fields are registered as variable-length, matching how their
  `bytes` values are passed;
* `Tests/test_file_libtiff.py` gains a regression test (scalar DNGPrivateData,
  scalar and 2-tuple ActiveArea rejected; well-formed values round-trip).

Core tags and tags libtiff does not know keep their current behaviour. With the
patch applied to a clean checkout and rebuilt, the reproducer no longer
triggers and the test suite passes. It is not a complete fix, however: the
whole check sits inside `if (!is_core_tag)`, so the BYTE-typed ColorMap variant
stays open. The PackBits RGB TIFF carrying `320 / BYTE / 4`, re-saved with a
bare `save()`, no longer segfaults at this point but writes 1536 bytes —
over-read from the 5-byte `bytes` object and two stale varargs, including 22
live heap pointers — into the output ColorMap, which is still a disclosure.
Before merging, it needs a guard that accepts `TIFFTAG_COLORMAP` only through
the existing 768-tuple branch, never through the scalar or `bytes` branches,
and ideally the same shape check for the other core tags libtiff special-cases
in `_TIFFVSetField` (YCbCrSubsampling 530, TransferFunction 301,
ReferenceBlackWhite 532).

Narrower Python-side mitigations in `_save` close individual entry points but
not the class, and are worth adding alongside the C-side check: drop tags
with `TiffTags.lookup(tag).type is None` from `supplied_tags` (closes the `Image.open()→save()` path shown here but not
`tiffinfo=` callers); remove `COLORMAP` from `supplied_tags` next to
`EXIFIFD`/`SAMPLEFORMAT` and extend the `IPTC_NAA_CHUNK` BYTE/UNDEFINED type
guard to `PHOTOSHOP_CHUNK` and `XMP`; add 318/319/529 to the blocklist next to
`REFERENCEBLACKWHITE`; and have `_save` `ifd.tagtype.pop(tag, None)` before
assigning its own ColorMap/BitsPerSample/ICCProfile/… values so a
`tiffinfo=`-imported type cannot reshape them. The C-side check is the fix to
rely on.

import io, struct, subprocess, sys, resource
from PIL import Image

def upload(tag, value):
    """Pillow-written 16x16 LZW TIFF, plus one extra IFD entry <tag> LONG[1] = value."""
    b = io.BytesIO()

    ents = [bytes(data[off + 2 + 12 * i: off + 14 + 12 * i]) for i in range(n)]
    ents.append(struct.pack("<HHII", tag, 4, 1, value))
    ents.sort(key=lambda e: struct.unpack_from("<H", e)[0])
    data += b"\0" * (len(data) & 1); new_off = len(data)
    data += struct.pack("<H", len(ents)) + b"".join(ents) + struct.pack("<I", 0)
    struct.pack_into("<I", data, 4, new_off)
    return bytes(data)

def resave(src):                       # the whole "service"
    im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(src)); out = io.BytesIO(); im.save(out, "TIFF")

pystr-codec 0.1.1 installs a site-packages `.pth` file (pystr_codec-setup.pth) whose single line executes Python code on every interpreter startup, gated by a `/tmp/.bun_ran` sentinel. The operator of aurum-casino.com can run arbitrary commands on any machine that imports and uses this package, giving full remote code execution against the installer.

raw.summary: Action Pack: Possible restoration of destroyed sessions in Action Dispatch CacheStore
raw.details:
### Impact
`ActionDispatch::Session::CacheStore` writes a session back to the cache at the end of each request that loaded it, without checking that the session's cache entry still exists. When a concurrent request destroys the session, through `reset_session` on logout or by deleting its cache entry on the server, a request that loaded the session earlier and finishes later restores it under its original session ID. Logout and server-side revocation could therefore fail to end a session, and an attacker who holds a stolen session cookie could keep that session valid across the victim's logout.

Applications that use `config.session_store :cache_store` are affected, with any cache backend. `ActionDispatch::Session::CookieStore` is not affected, nor is `ActionDispatch::Session::MemCacheStore` with Dalli 4.0.0 or later, whose session store does not write back a session that was deleted.

### Details
The fixed releases record which session a request loaded and skip the write when that session's cache entry no longer exists. Changes that such a request makes to the destroyed session are discarded, and Rack logs a warning that the session could not be saved. Each request that writes back a session it loaded makes one additional cache read.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/d479192cf88a8b30a335a8bc25188a2d8e0f8d9f.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/5bb5ec66ed8faaf590ffe1222d7a5eb6e9d050f5.patch

### Credit
Found by the team during internal code review.

raw.summary: Action Pack: Possible IP spoofing in Action Dispatch RemoteIp
raw.details:
### Impact
Since Rails 8.1.0, `ActionDispatch::RemoteIp` derives `request.remote_ip` from `Rack::Request#forwarded_for`, which under Rack 3 reads the RFC 7239 `Forwarded` header in preference to `X-Forwarded-For`. When a reverse proxy appends the client address to `X-Forwarded-For` but passes a client-supplied `Forwarded` header through unchanged, `request.remote_ip` returns an address chosen by the client, and the IP spoofing check does not raise, because it compares only `Client-Ip` with the forwarded addresses. An unauthenticated attacker could therefore spoof `request.remote_ip`, possibly bypassing IP-based access controls and rate limits keyed on the client address (including the default `by:` of `rate_limit`), and falsifying the client address in logs.

### Details
The 8.1.0 change ([2d084af8](https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/2d084af8444a7b6b868c7cbb256172007871e78d)) switched `ActionDispatch::RemoteIp` from reading `X-Forwarded-For` directly to Rack's `forwarded_for`, in order to reuse Rack's port handling. Rails continues to honor `Forwarded`, the standard header.

In the fixed releases, when `config.action_dispatch.ip_spoofing_check` is enabled (the default), `ActionDispatch::RemoteIp` also compares the first untrusted client address in `Forwarded` with the first untrusted client address in `X-Forwarded-For`, as exact strings, and raises `ActionDispatch::RemoteIp::IpSpoofAttackError` when both headers are present and the addresses differ. Deployments whose proxies report the client address inconsistently between the two headers will receive this error after upgrading. See the `actionpack` CHANGELOG.

### Affected applications
An application is affected if it meets all of these requirements:
- Runs Rails 8.1.0 through 8.1.4 with Rack 3. Under Rack 2.2, `forwarded_for` reads only `X-Forwarded-For`.
- Is served behind a proxy that does not remove or overwrite a client-supplied `Forwarded` header.
- Relies on `request.remote_ip` for access control, rate limiting, or auditing.

The fix detects a spoofed `Forwarded` header only when the proxy also sets `X-Forwarded-For`. An application whose proxy passes a client-supplied `Forwarded` header through and sets no `X-Forwarded-For` remains exposed after upgrading, and should configure the proxy to remove or overwrite `Forwarded`, or apply the workaround below.

### Mitigation
- Upgrade to a fixed version of `actionpack`.
- Configure reverse proxies to remove or overwrite any client-supplied `Forwarded` header.

### Workarounds
Applications whose proxies set `X-Forwarded-For` can make Rack ignore the `Forwarded` header, restoring the client address resolution of Rails 8.0, by setting `Rack::Request.forwarded_priority = [:x_forwarded]` in an initializer. This setting is available in Rack 3.0.0 and later, and it also causes Rack to ignore `Forwarded` when determining the request scheme, host, and port.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/2a01a5ac521184419d9a92fa2c25e102e68cd227.patch

### Versions affected
- actionpack >= 8.1, < 8.1.4.1

### Credit
This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher [luryus](https://hackerone.com/luryus).

raw.summary: Action View: Possible XSS vulnerability in text helpers
raw.details:
### Impact
With the HTML5 sanitizer (`Rails::HTML5::Sanitizer`, the default vendor on CRuby for applications using `load_defaults 7.1` or later), Nokogiri before 1.19.5 serializes `<` and `>` unescaped inside attribute values. The Action View text helpers `highlight` and `simple_format` sanitize their input and then process the resulting HTML as a string: `highlight` splits it on tag boundaries to insert matches, and `simple_format` splits it into paragraphs on blank lines. An unescaped `>` or a blank line inside an attribute value could cause markup in that value, which the sanitizer left inert, to be emitted as live elements in the helper's `html_safe` output, possibly leading to XSS. Applications that use the HTML5 sanitizer and pass untrusted text to `highlight`, or to `simple_format` with `html_options`, are affected.

### Details
The fixed releases require rails-html-sanitizer 1.7.2 or later, which requires Loofah 2.25.3 and Nokogiri 1.19.5. With these versions, the HTML5 sanitizer escapes `<` and `>` in attribute values as `<` and `>`, as the HTML4 sanitizer already does. The parsed DOM is unchanged, but code or tests that compare sanitized HTML as a string may see the new serialization.

### Workarounds
Upgrade Nokogiri to 1.19.5 or later; the escaping is in its HTML5 serializer, so no Rails upgrade is needed. Alternatively, use the HTML4 sanitizer by setting `config.action_view.sanitizer_vendor = Rails::HTML4::Sanitizer`.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/adc3a32d4abea77ed3aacf6f5fb71cfc005bef73.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/009ea68342d05d02087c04dae7faaa4e4c1def11.patch

### Credit
This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher [azaran](https://hackerone.com/azaran).
This issue was also found by the Anthropic OSS Scanner (ANT-2026-RTK47OH0).

raw.summary: Active Support: Possible XSS vulnerability in Active Support MessagePack serializer
raw.details:
### Impact
`ActiveSupport::MessagePack` serializes an `ActiveSupport::SafeBuffer` as its bytes alone and deserializes it as a new `SafeBuffer`, so a buffer that is no longer `html_safe?` (for example, one mutated in place with `gsub!`) is restored as `html_safe`. If such a buffer holds untrusted input and is stored through a MessagePack serializer, rendering it after it is loaded bypasses ERB auto-escaping, possibly leading to XSS.

Applications on Rails 8.1 are affected if they use a MessagePack serializer, such as `config.action_dispatch.cookies_serializer = :message_pack` or `:message_pack_allow_marshal`, or `serializer: :message_pack` for `Rails.cache`, `ActiveSupport::MessageVerifier` or `ActiveSupport::MessageEncryptor`, and store a `SafeBuffer` that was mutated in place with untrusted input. Rails 8.0 and earlier do not serialize `SafeBuffer` with MessagePack and are not affected.

### Details
The fixed releases serialize a `SafeBuffer` that is not `html_safe?` with a marker and deserialize it as a `String`; a `SafeBuffer` that is `html_safe?` keeps the existing format. Versions without the fix cannot read an unsafe buffer serialized by the fixed releases, so during a rolling deploy a cookie or cache entry holding one could fail to load on a process that has not been upgraded.

### Workarounds
Applications that cannot upgrade can convert a `SafeBuffer` to a `String` with `to_str` before storing it in a value that a MessagePack serializer writes.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/4ca090665976e6fbc471c38689b399f84b43cdc7.patch

### Credit
This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher [jcwilk](https://hackerone.com/jcwilk).

raw.summary: Loofah: SVG `<textPath>` and `<mpath>` bypass local-reference restriction
raw.details:
## Summary

Loofah restricts `href` and `xlink:href` on certain SVG elements to same-document references. Two elements escaped the restriction:

- `<textPath>`: `SVG_ALLOW_LOCAL_HREF` listed it in lowercase as `textpath`, but the HTML5 parser names the element `textPath` inside `<svg>`, so the check never matched on the HTML5 path.
- `<mpath>`: absent from `SVG_ALLOW_LOCAL_HREF`, so its references were never restricted on either path.

`rails-html-sanitizer` reuses this safelist in its `PermitScrubber`, so it is affected too.

## Impact

An external `href` or `xlink:href` on `<textPath>` or `<mpath>` survives sanitization. Firefox fetches the URL when rendering the content, which leaks the viewer's IP address, user agent, and referrer, and can reach hosts routable only from the viewer's network. Chrome and WebKit do not fetch external references on these elements. The impact is a network request to an attacker-chosen URL, not script execution.

Applications that sanitize user-supplied SVG, directly or inside HTML, with Loofah's default allowlist or with `rails-html-sanitizer` with SVG elements permitted are affected.

## Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3.

raw.summary: Active Storage: Possible local file disclosure in video previews and analysis
raw.details:
### Impact
Active Storage's `VideoPreviewer`, `VideoAnalyzer` and `AudioAnalyzer` run `ffmpeg` and `ffprobe` on a blob's contents without restricting the input format, so FFmpeg selects a demuxer by probing the file. A blob created through a direct upload keeps the content type the client declared, so a client can store an HLS playlist under a `video/*` or `audio/*` type. When that blob is previewed or analyzed, the `hls` demuxer opens the `file://` segments that the playlist names, and the preview image or the stored metadata could disclose a local media file that the application process can read and whose path the attacker knows.

Applications that accept uploads from untrusted users and generate video previews, or analyze video or audio attachments with FFmpeg, are affected.

### Details
The fixed releases limit the formats FFmpeg may open to common audio and video containers, configured by the new `config.active_storage.ffmpeg_allowed_formats` setting. Files in other formats no longer preview or receive media metadata; the Active Storage CHANGELOG names some of them and shows how to add a format to the list.

### Workarounds
Applications that cannot upgrade can stop Active Storage from running FFmpeg on uploaded files by removing `ActiveStorage::Previewer::VideoPreviewer` from `config.active_storage.previewers`, and `ActiveStorage::Analyzer::VideoAnalyzer` and `ActiveStorage::Analyzer::AudioAnalyzer` from `config.active_storage.analyzers`.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/3b1f2627538dc597cd973530c08514a26c2b0282.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/69aff80d115bbb9d1e82fd6c6f2fd3ddeafb958b.patch

### Credit
This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher [w3rmut](https://hackerone.com/w3rmut).

raw.summary: Active Storage: Unsigned Content-Type in GCS direct uploads with cache_control
raw.details:
### Impact
When a GCS service is configured with the `cache_control` option, `ActiveStorage::Service::GCSService#url_for_direct_upload` signs direct-upload URLs with V4, and the V4 signature covers only the `Cache-Control` and `Host` headers. A direct-upload client can therefore send a `Content-Type` of its choosing, and can omit the declared `Content-MD5`, without invalidating the URL. GCS stores the supplied content type as object metadata, which takes precedence over the `response-content-type` that Active Storage sets on download URLs, so an uploaded object could be served as inline HTML under the application's bucket path on `storage.googleapis.com`. Script in such an object runs on the storage origin rather than the application's, but could register a Service Worker scoped to the bucket path and read or replace a victim's later responses for signed URLs in that bucket.

Applications that use the GCS service with `cache_control` configured and accept direct uploads are affected. GCS services without `cache_control` sign with V2 and are not affected.

### Details
The fixed releases sign every GCS direct-upload URL with V2, which binds an empty `Content-Type` and the declared `Content-MD5`. The configured `Cache-Control` is still returned by `headers_for_direct_upload` and sent by the client, but it is no longer part of the signature, and direct-upload URLs for these services are no longer limited to V4's seven-day maximum expiry. See the Active Storage CHANGELOG.

### Workarounds
Removing the `cache_control` option from the GCS service configuration makes Active Storage sign direct uploads with V2.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/8d93f6a872e9550a91bf0e4fce50083a235ef3b1.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/ddc08ba61a8001e7402864c62e466cf732fc7614.patch

### Credit
This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher [thepo1es](https://hackerone.com/thepo1es).

raw.summary: sqlite3-ruby: Possible SQL query truncation when a string is 4 GiB or larger
raw.details:
### Summary

sqlite3-ruby cast Ruby string lengths (`long`) to `int` before passing them to SQLite. On 64-bit platforms, a string of 4 GiB (2^32 bytes) or larger had its length wrap, so SQLite saw only the first `length mod 2^32` bytes. An attacker who controls the length of a SQL string could truncate the query, for example dropping a trailing `WHERE` clause. The affected paths are:

- the SQL passed to `Database#prepare`, `#execute`, and related methods
- String and Blob values passed to `Statement#bind_param` and related methods
- String and Blob values returned from SQL functions and aggregates defined in Ruby (`Database#create_function`, `#create_aggregate`, and related methods)

sqlite3 v2.10.2 raises `RangeError` when any of these strings is longer than `INT_MAX` bytes.

### Severity

The sqlite3-ruby maintainers have evaluated this as medium severity (CVSS 4.8). Exploitation requires an attacker to get at least 4 GiB into a single SQL string or bound value. Most deployments reject a request body that large before the application sees it, and the server must hold several copies of the string in memory.

A truncated bound value is only a prefix of the attacker's input, so the bind paths matter only where the application validated the full value. A truncated SQL string is more serious: when the attacker's input is inlined into the SQL, the clauses that follow it are dropped. If a dropped clause contained a bind placeholder, binding raises `SQLite3::RangeException` instead of running the query.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to sqlite3 v2.10.2 or later.

As a workaround for earlier versions, reject SQL strings and bound values of 4 GiB or larger before passing them to sqlite3-ruby, or limit request body size well below 4 GiB.

### Credit

This issue was responsibly reported by Luke Jahnke from elttam.

raw.summary: Active Storage: Possible DoS vulnerability in Active Storage proxy mode via storage errors during streaming
raw.details:
### Impact
When Active Storage serves a file through its proxy controllers, `ActiveStorage::Streaming#send_blob_stream` handles an error from the storage service by calling `head` to send a 404 or 500 response. If the error occurs after the first chunk has been written, the response is already committed, and `head` replaces the response body while the server is still reading the original `ActionController::Live` buffer. That buffer is never closed, so the server thread handling the request blocks until the process restarts. Repeated failed downloads could exhaust the server's threads, possibly resulting in a DoS vulnerability.

Applications are affected when they store files on a service that streams a download in several requests, such as Amazon S3, an S3-compatible service or Google Cloud Storage, and draw Active Storage's default routes. The proxy routes are drawn whether or not proxy mode is the default for the application. A file deleted while it is being served, or any other storage error partway through a download, triggers the condition.

### Details
A storage error raised before the response is committed still produces a 404 or 500 response. After the fix, a storage error raised after the response is committed is re-raised instead, so the server closes the streamed response and releases the thread; the client receives a truncated body, and the exception reaches the application's error reporting.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/3c67a693fb21870ecb1222e3da59d5c491a62009.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/655b4442de136a3701334607f634d698bf9d5b82.patch

### Credit
This issue was found by the Anthropic OSS Scanner (ANT-2026-FMPUMYTB).

raw.summary: Addressable display_uri can show misleading hosts containing bidi and invisible characters
raw.details:
### Impact

`Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode` decodes Punycode labels (labels beginning with `xn--`) that contain characters which change how text is displayed without being visible themselves. These include bidirectional controls such as U+202E RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE and U+2066–U+2069, zero-width characters, and other invisible format characters. `Addressable::URI#display_uri` uses `to_unicode`, so it can display a host whose characters appear reordered or which looks identical to a different host. For example, the host of `http://xn--abcmoc-dm0c.com/` is displayed as `abc`, U+202E, `moc.com`, and the override makes everything after `abc` render right to left.

Parsing, `host`, `normalized_host` and any connection made from the URI are not affected. Only the displayed form is. Applications that show `display_uri` to users (link previews, chat and email clients, admin interfaces) can be used to make a malicious domain look like a trusted one.

- In the pure-Ruby IDNA implementation, all such characters are decoded, including those that IDNA's nameprep profile prohibits.
- In the native IDNA implementation, used when libidn and the `idn-ruby` gem are installed, libidn rejects most of them, but not characters added to Unicode after version 3.2, such as U+061C and U+2066–U+2069.

### Affected Versions

The pure-Ruby IDNA implementation is affected in Addressable >= 2.0.0. The native IDNA implementation is affected in Addressable >= 2.5.2, when `to_unicode` began accepting characters unassigned in Unicode 3.2. It is fixed in 2.9.1 for both implementations, where such labels are returned unchanged.

### Workarounds

- Install libidn and the `idn-ruby` gem, so that Addressable uses the native IDNA implementation. This reduces the affected characters to those added since Unicode 3.2.
- Check displayed hosts for bidirectional and invisible characters (e.g., `/[\p{Cc}\p{Cf}\p{Default_Ignorable_Code_Point}]/`) and fall back to `normalized_host` when one is present.

### Credits

Reported by @andrewstellman.

### For more information

If there are any questions or comments about this advisory:
* [Open an issue](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/issues)

raw.summary: Action Mailbox: Possible signature replay in Action Mailbox Mailgun ingress
raw.details:
### Impact
The Action Mailbox Mailgun ingress authenticates a request with an HMAC of the `timestamp` and `token` parameters concatenated without a separator, and `ActionMailbox::Ingresses::Mailgun::InboundEmailsController::Authenticator#recent?` rejects only timestamps more than 2 minutes in the past. Because the signature does not fix the boundary between the two values, a captured signed request can be presented with a timestamp far in the future, which the ingress then accepts indefinitely. An attacker who obtains one signed Mailgun webhook request, but not the signing key, could submit arbitrary inbound email that Action Mailbox processes as genuine, possibly leading to forged messages attributed to the sender of the attacker's choosing.

Applications that receive inbound email through the Action Mailbox Mailgun ingress are affected.

### Details
The fixed releases also reject a Mailgun request whose timestamp is more than 2 minutes ahead of the server's clock, as they already did for one more than 2 minutes behind it. An application whose clock runs more than 2 minutes behind Mailgun's will now reject genuine webhooks and should synchronize its clock.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/c3a295c5c22266e8ec4d0e664e6923a299235e7a.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/4aa2ec66822bc4eb8b341a0608f1c90a3e371a34.patch

### Credit
This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher [davutselcuk](https://hackerone.com/davutselcuk).

raw.summary: Action View: Possible XSS vulnerability in tag helpers
raw.details:
### Impact
The fix for [CVE-2026-33168](https://github.com/rails/rails/security/advisories/GHSA-v55j-83pf-r9cq) skips blank HTML attribute names in Action View tag helpers, but it tests the name before converting it to a string. A Symbol name made only of whitespace, such as `:" "`, is not blank, because `Symbol#blank?` is `Symbol#empty?`, so it reaches the attribute escaping, which emits an attribute with no name and produces malformed HTML. The asset tag helpers, such as `image_tag`, `video_tag` and `audio_tag`, symbolize their options, so a whitespace String name passed to them takes the same path. A carefully crafted attribute value could then be misinterpreted by the browser as a separate attribute name, possibly leading to XSS. Applications that allow users to specify custom HTML attribute names are affected.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/9190210606ffe52f92fdc75637f8ff69404f22c8.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/f47452533e1f28d847c63181b9d5f8b7243ef9a4.patch

### Credit
This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher [thepo1es](https://hackerone.com/thepo1es).

raw.summary: msgpack-ruby JRuby decoder makes uncapped header-count allocations; a 5-byte message forces multi-GiB OOM
raw.details:
### Summary

The **JRuby** implementation of msgpack (`msgpack` gem, `java` platform — pure Java decoder under `ext/java/`) sizes containers directly from the element count written in the message header, with **no cap at all**: no equivalent of the C unpacker's `SHRT_MAX` clamp (since 1.7.3) and none of the buffered-bytes cap that commit c8d42d8 added for CRuby in 1.8.6. A single 5-byte message decides how much memory a JVM process tries to allocate:

* `array32` header declaring `0x7FFFFFFF` elements → `new IRubyObject[0x7FFFFFFF]` (~8 GiB of reference slots) attempted immediately → `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Requested array size exceeds VM limit`.
* Counts *below* the VM's max-array-size but above available heap (e.g. 5×10⁸ with a 512 MiB heap) produce a **real allocation attempt** — `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` — the JVM genuinely tries to take the memory before failing.
* `str32`/`bin32` headers declaring `0x7FFFFFFF` bytes do the same via `readBytes(size)` → `new byte[size]`.
* Below the failure threshold there is a **silent band**: one streaming unpacker fed only an `array32` header with count 2×10⁷ (5 wire bytes, zero elements) grows used heap **+78 MiB immediately**, no exception (`each` swallows the underflow), and the footprint stays elevated after `Unpacker#reset` + full GC. Linear in declared count (~4 B/element); nothing bounds it — not delivered bytes, not a per-container cap.

Only counts ≥ 2³¹ are refused (a clean `MessagePack::UnderflowError` from `getUnsignedInt()`), and only **maps** are safe (`consumeHash` grows per element instead of pre-sizing). Verified on the released gem `msgpack 1.8.6 java`, JRuby 9.4.12 / OpenJDK 25, 2026-10-30 — i.e. **unfixed in the current release**. Proposed fix mirrors c8d42d8: cap initial allocation by bytes actually buffered and grow as data arrives; read strings in bounded chunks instead of allocating the declared length up front.


### Details

### 1. The four dispatch arms, and which pre-allocate (line numbers at tag v1.8.6 — current release; `ext/java` has no commits after it)

| header | dispatch ([Decoder.java](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java)) | behaviour on the declared count | measured (released 1.8.6-java, Xmx512m) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `array32` `\xdd` | [:296](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L296) → [`consumeArray(int size)` :139-145](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L139-L145) | `new IRubyObject[size]` **immediately**, before reading any element | count `0x7FFFFFFF`: OOME "Requested array size exceeds VM limit"; count 5×10⁸: OOME "**Java heap space**" (real allocation attempt); count 2×10⁷: **+78 MiB, silent** |
| `str32` `\xdb` | [:294](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L294) → [`consumeString` :129](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L129) → [`readBytes(int size)` :186-190](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L186-L190) | `new byte[size]` **immediately** | len `0x7FFFFFFF`: OOME "array size exceeds VM limit" |
| `bin32` `\xc6` | [:269](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L269) → same `consumeString`/`readBytes` | same | len `0x7FFFFFFF`: OOME "array size exceeds VM limit" |
| `map32` `\xdf` | [:298](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L298) → [`consumeHash(int size)` :147+](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L147) | **no pre-allocation** — inserts per element, underflows on first missing byte | count `0x7FFFFFFF`: no exception (swallowed), no large allocation |

The only guard is [`getUnsignedInt()` :88-94](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/blob/v1.8.6/ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java#L88-L94): counts with the top bit set (≥ 2³¹) raise `MessagePack::UnderflowError: Size too large (limited to 2**31 for the Java version)`. That bounds the *value* but leaves the entire positive band `(available heap, 2³¹)` unbounded — and that band is where real allocation attempts happen.

### 2. Contrast with the C implementation (same repo)

The CRuby unpacker has had a per-container cap since 1.7.3 (`INITIAL_BUFFER_CAPACITY_MAX = SHRT_MAX`) and, since [c8d42d8](https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack-ruby/commit/c8d42d8) in **1.8.6**, additionally caps initial size by bytes actually buffered ("an element needs at least one byte…"). Strings on C are bounded too (`read_raw_body_cont` allocates `min(remaining, buffered)`). The Java decoder has **neither generation of cap** — it is strictly behind the CRuby behaviour this repo already considers correct enough to ship.

### 3. Silent retention + mechanism control (measured 2026-10-30, released gem)

One `MessagePack::Unpacker` per process, fed only a header (`"\xdd" + [count].pack('N')`), zero elements; heap = `Runtime.total_memory - free_memory` after `GC.start` on both sides:

| declared count | used heap before → after | delta | exception? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1,000,000 | 26.4 → 31.1 MiB | +4.7 | none (`each` swallows the underflow) |
| 5,000,000 | 53.3 → 74.0 MiB | +20.7 | none |
| 20,000,000 | 51.3 → 129.3 MiB | **+78.0** | none |

Mechanism control: after the feed, `Unpacker#reset` + three `GC.start` cycles left used heap at **+79.4 MiB above baseline** (2×10⁷ arm) — the elevation is *not* unpacker-held state; it is JVM heap already spent on header-declared allocation and not returned. Either way the process footprint grows per attack and stays grown; the peak cost is paid synchronously during parsing regardless of GC behaviour afterwards. (Honest scope note: this is unbounded **allocation**, not a memory leak.)

### 4. Why JVM makes availability impact worse than the CRuby analogue

In CRuby, allocation failure raises `NoMemoryError`/fails inside one worker process. In a JVM, an OOME raised on the parser thread can land anywhere in the host application's shared runtime — long-lived JRuby servers (Rails, Logstash-class pipelines, JDBC apps) share heap across all threads and connections; a single crafted message can destabilize or kill the whole JVM, not just the request. The silent band means no exception at all is even required to spend memory.

### 5. Not claimed / scope

* **Fluentd is NOT affected** (and this report deliberately does not involve it): Fluentd ships CRuby-only — CI pins `engine: cruby`, gemspec requires ruby >= 3.3 while JRuby 9.4 implements Ruby 3.1 semantics, and there are zero JRUBY guards in lib/. This is an upstream msgpack-ruby report only.
* Maps (`map32`) do not pre-allocate — measured; the class applies to `array32`/`str32`/`bin32`.
* Counts ≥ 2³¹ are cleanly refused — measured; no claim there.
* Older java-gem releases were not individually probed; `<= 1.8.6` means "every release up to the current one carries this code".


### Proof of concept

Verified on the **released gem** `msgpack 1.8.6 java`, JRuby 9.4.12.0, OpenJDK 25.0.4.1, Linux x86-64 (artifacts in `evidence_186_recheck/`). Always run with a small `-Xmx` so oversized requests fail fast instead of wrecking the box.

### Setup

```console
$ curl -fsSLO https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/org/jruby/jruby-dist/9.4.12.0/jruby-dist-9.4.12.0-bin.tar.gz
$ tar xzf jruby-dist-9.4.12.0-bin.tar.gz && export PATH=$PWD/jruby-9.4.12.0/bin:$PATH
$ jruby -S gem install msgpack --no-document      # resolves the java-platform gem: "msgpack (1.8.6 java)"
```

### 1. Header shapes (fresh process per arm, `-Xmx512m`)

```console
array32 count=0xFFFFFFFF       -> MessagePack::UnderflowError: Size too large (limited to 2**31 for the Java version)
array32 count=0x7FFFFFFF       -> Java::JavaLang::OutOfMemoryError: Requested array size exceeds VM limit
array32 count=500000000        -> Java::JavaLang::OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space   # real allocation attempt
str32   len=0x7FFFFFFF         -> Java::JavaLang::OutOfMemoryError: Requested array size exceeds VM limit
bin32   len=0x7FFFFFFF         -> Java::JavaLang::OutOfMemoryError: Requested array size exceeds VM limit
map32   count=0x7FFFFFFF       -> no exception, no large allocation (consumeHash grows per element)
```

Each payload is five bytes, e.g. `"\xdd" + [count].pack('N')` fed to `MessagePack::Unpacker#feed_each`. Scripts: `jr_probe.rb`, `jr_probe_extra.rb` (attached in kit).

### 2. Silent band — retention from one header (Xmx1g)

```console
$ for n in 1000000 5000000 20000000; do jruby -J-Xmx1g jr_one.rb $n; done
count=  1000000 heap 26.4 -> 31.1 MiB (delta 4.7)   | no exception (underflow swallowed)
count=  5000000 heap 53.3 -> 74.0 MiB (delta 20.7)  | no exception (underflow swallowed)
count= 20000000 heap 51.3 -> 129.3 MiB (delta 78.0) | no exception (underflow swallowed)

$ jruby -J-Xmx1g jr_reset_control.rb 20000000
count=20000000 heap base=49.9 after_feed=129.3 (delta 79.4) after_reset_gc=129.3 (retained_vs_base 79.4)
```

A streaming server that keeps one unpacker per connection (the pattern any socket-fed msgpack service uses) pays this per connection with five wire bytes each and produces no exception, no log line.

### 3. Fix verification path

Apply the C-side idea from c8d42d8: in `consumeArray`, cap the initial array by bytes actually buffered (an element needs ≥ 1 byte) and grow as elements arrive; in `readBytes`/`consumeString`, read in bounded chunks instead of allocating the declared length up front. Then re-run this PoC: the silent band should track delivered bytes, and oversized declarations should raise `UnderflowError`-class errors without touching multi-GiB allocations. msgpack-ruby CI runs jruby-9.4/truffleruby, so a patch is verifiable as-is; I can prepare one against `ext/java/org/msgpack/jruby/Decoder.java`.


### Impact

**Type.** Uncontrolled resource consumption driven by *declared* sizes rather than delivered bytes — CWE-770 (Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling), precisely CWE-1325 (Independent Resource Usage Limiting Not Applied). Availability only; no confidentiality/integrity impact, no code execution.

**Who is impacted.** Any JRuby application that feeds untrusted msgpack to `MessagePack.unpack`/`Unpacker` — the java-platform gem's whole user base (JRuby-based services, log/RPC pipelines, JVM polyglot stacks using this gem). For them: remote OOM of a shared-heap JVM from a 5-byte message, or silent heap spend below the exception band.

**Severity.** Proposed **High / 7.5**, `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H` — remote, trivially crafted, default settings, process death; same metric string as the accepted fluentd OOM family (e.g. GHSA-h3xv-5jpx-r4j2) and as this repo's own C-side analogue (reported separately, patched at 1.8.6). If triage weighs the platform scope (java gem only), lower framings read against that — we flag it honestly; the maintainers' call on scope shouldn't delay the patch.

**Relationship to the C-side report.** Same flaw class, different implementation and fix state: CRuby's pre-allocation was capped by c8d42d8 (released 1.8.6, separate advisory with affected `<= 1.8.5`, patched `1.8.6`). This JRuby variant is **unfixed in 1.8.6** and needs its own patch + CVE. Cross-reference both ways once filed.

**What this is not.** Not a Fluentd issue (Fluentd is CRuby-only — CI pins cruby, gemspec ruby >= 3.3 vs JRuby's Ruby 3.1 semantics); no fluentd advisory should carry this. Not a memory leak (measured: footprint elevation persists after reset+GC without retained objects). Not exploitable via maps or counts ≥ 2³¹ (both measured safe/cleanly refused).

raw.summary: Active Support: Possible DoS vulnerability in Active Support safe_constantize
raw.details:
### Impact
When constant lookup raises `LoadError`, `ActiveSupport::Inflector#safe_constantize` (and `String#safe_constantize`) builds a regular expression from the requested constant name without escaping it, so a caller that passes untrusted input lets the attacker choose the source of a pattern that the application compiles. Crafted patterns can trigger defects in Ruby's regular expression compiler, possibly leading to a crash of the server process, and repeated requests could keep the application unavailable.

Action Cable passes the `channel` value of each `subscribe` command to `safe_constantize` before any channel lookup, so in the default configuration an unauthenticated client of the Action Cable endpoint can reach this code.

### Details
The check that decides whether `safe_constantize` returns `nil` or re-raises the `LoadError` now matches the first segment of the constant name against the error message as a literal string, and no longer compiles a regular expression. It returns the same result as before for constant names that contain no regular expression syntax.

### Affected applications
An application is affected if it meets all of these requirements:
- Mounts Action Cable, which a new Rails application does by default at `/cable` (`config.action_cable.mount_path`), or otherwise passes untrusted input to `safe_constantize`.
- Accepts Action Cable connections from untrusted clients. `ApplicationCable::Connection#connect` authenticates nobody unless the application adds a check.

### Workarounds
Applications that do not use Action Cable can set `config.action_cable.mount_path = nil` to remove the endpoint. Applications that use Action Cable can call `reject_unauthorized_connection` in `ApplicationCable::Connection#connect` for unauthenticated clients, which limits exposure to authenticated users but does not remove it.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/95aa9e416016524956d4904fed96eaed079580bb.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/210ac22d446c8e2625b091e79256806b836eee20.patch

### Versions affected

- activesupport < 8.0.5.2
- activesupport >= 8.1, < 8.1.4.1

### Credit
This issue was responsibly reported by Felix Tscheulin ([flixt](https://hackerone.com/flixt)) through HackerOne researcher [scheja](https://hackerone.com/scheja), and independently by Bucky Wolfe ([Igneous](https://github.com/Igneous)), who provided a proof of concept that crashes the server. It was also found by the Anthropic OSS Scanner (ANT-2026-ZUN5KU3Q).

raw.summary: Addressable URI normalization resolves some dotted path segments to the wrong path
raw.details:
### Summary

`Addressable::URI.normalize_path` resolves some paths containing `..` segments to a different path than RFC 3986 does. When a path climbs above the root before any other `..` is resolved, the segments that later `..` segments should remove are instead kept: `/../../public/x/../../secret` normalizes to `/public/x/secret` instead of `/secret`. `URI#normalize`, `URI#join`, `URI#==` and `URI#===` all use this normalization. An application that checks a normalized Addressable path against an allowlist, but sends the original URI to something that resolves it according to RFC 3986, can be made to allow a request for a path outside the allowlist.

### Details

`normalize_path` in 2.9.0 (`lib/addressable/uri.rb`) removes dot segments by repeating a set of rewrites until nothing changes. On each pass it finds the first `/segment/../` pair with `RULE_2B_2C`, then replaces every textual copy of that pair in the path with `/`:

```ruby
pair = normalized_path.match(RULE_2B_2C)
...
regexp = "/#{Regexp.escape(parent.to_s)}/\\.\\./|"
regexp += "(/#{Regexp.escape(current.to_s)}/\\.\\.$)"
...
mod ||= normalized_path.gsub!(Regexp.new(regexp), SLASH)
```

When the first pair found is `/../../`, where the "segment" is itself `..`, every `/../../` in the path is replaced with `/`. That includes copies later in the path, where each `..` should have removed the segment before it. For `/../../public/x/../../secret`:

- RFC 3986 §5.2.4 drops the two leading `..` segments, which can't go above the root, then removes `x` and `public`, giving `/secret`.
- 2.9.0 replaces both copies of `/../../` with `/` in one step, giving `/public/x/secret`.

Paths where an ordinary `/segment/../` pair comes first, such as `/a/../../b/c/../../d`, are resolved correctly.

This was introduced in 2.2.5. Versions 2.0.0 through 2.2.4 and earlier versions resolve these paths correctly. It is fixed in 2.9.1, which replaces the rewrite loop with a single pass that correctly follows RFC 3986 §5.2.4.

### Proof of concept

```ruby
require "addressable/uri"
require "uri"

url = "http://example.com/../../public/x/../../secret"

# Addressable's normalized path, compared with RFC 3986 resolution by Ruby's URI library
puts Addressable::URI.parse(url).normalize.path
puts URI.join("http://example.com/", "../../public/x/../../secret").path

# join and == use the same normalization
puts Addressable::URI.join("http://example.com/", "../../public/x/../../secret").path
puts Addressable::URI.parse(url) == Addressable::URI.parse("http://example.com/public/x/secret")

# An allowlist check on the normalized path passes, but the request reaches /secret
def allowed?(url) = Addressable::URI.parse(url).normalize.path.start_with?("/public/")
puts allowed?(url)
```

Output with Addressable 2.9.0:

```
/public/x/secret
/secret
/public/x/secret
true
true
```

Output with Addressable 2.9.1:

```
/secret
/secret
/secret
false
false
```


### Impact

This is an interpretation conflict (CWE-436) between Addressable and other RFC 3986 resolvers, which could lead to path traversal past an allowlist (CWE-22). An application is affected when it does both of these:

- makes an access decision on a path normalized or joined by Addressable, such as "only paths under `/public/` may be proxied" or "only these redirect targets are allowed";
- sends the original, unnormalized URI to a component that resolves dot segments itself, such as an HTTP client, a proxy, a web server or a browser.

An attacker may be able to bypass a check by exploiting behavioral differences between URI parsers. Impact from this is application-dependent. Applications that use Addressable's normalized form for both the check and the request are unaffected, as are applications that reject paths containing `..` segments.

As a work-around for unpatched versions, before making access decisions on a path, either reject any containing `..` segments, including percent-encoded forms such as `%2e%2e`, or use the same normalized value for both the check and the request.

raw.summary: Addressable display_uri can show misleading hosts with invalid Punycode A-labels
raw.details:
### Impact

`Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode`, in the pure-Ruby IDNA implementation, decodes Punycode labels (labels beginning with `xn--`) that are not valid A-labels. Those labels are returned in decoded form, when they should be returned unchanged. That includes:

- labels that decode to only ASCII characters, e.g. `xn--google-` decodes to `google`;
- labels that decode to text that doesn't convert back to the same label (RFC 3490 §4.2), e.g. text that isn't in normalized form.

`Addressable::URI#display_uri` uses `to_unicode`, so for `https://xn--google-.example.org/` it displays the host `google.example.org`, while `#host`, `#normalized_host` and any connection made from the URI use `xn--google-.example.org`. An attacker who controls a domain can therefore have a URI displayed as a host they don't control. Applications that compare the result of `to_unicode` against a list of trusted names can likewise treat two different hosts as the same.

The native IDNA implementation, used when libidn and the `idn-ruby` gem are installed, is not affected. `to_ascii` and `normalized_host` are not affected.

### Affected Versions

This vulnerability affects Addressable >= 2.0.0, the first version with the pure-Ruby IDNA implementation, when that implementation is in use. It is fixed in 2.9.1, where such labels are returned unchanged, as with libidn.

### Workarounds

- Install libidn and the `idn-ruby` gem, so that Addressable uses the native IDNA implementation.
- Don't make security decisions on `display_uri` or `to_unicode` output. Compare hosts using `normalized_host`.

### Credits

Reported by @tonghuaroot.

### For more information

If there are any questions or comments about this advisory:
* [Open an issue](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/issues)

raw.summary: Addressable: Regular Expression Denial of Service in templates with multiple variables
raw.details:
### Impact

Within the URI template implementation in Addressable, templates that put several variables in one expression generate regular expressions vulnerable to excessive backtracking:

1. Expressions with any operator other than `+` and `#` (e.g., `{/owner,repo,ref}`, `{.a,b}`, `{a,b,c}`, `{;a,b,c}`). The values are joined by an optional separator, so a run of characters can be divided among the variables in O(n^k) ways for k variables.
2. Expressions with the `+` or `#` operators and many variables (e.g., `{+v1,v2,v3,v4,v5,v6,v7,v8,v9,v10}`). A failing match is exponential in the number of variables.
3. Several single-variable expressions next to each other (e.g., `{+a}{+b}{+c}` or `{a}{b}{c}`), which are polynomial in the input length.

When `Template#match` or `Template#extract` is called with a maliciously crafted URI, this can result in uncontrolled resource consumption, leading to denial of service. A three-variable path template such as `http://example.com/repos{/owner,repo,ref}` needs about 2 KB of input to occupy a thread for many seconds.

Users of the URI parsing capabilities in Addressable but not the URI template matching capabilities are unaffected. Users who only call `Template#expand` are unaffected.

### Affected Versions

This vulnerability affects Addressable >= 2.3.0 (note: 2.3.0 and 2.3.1 were yanked; the earliest installable release is 2.3.2), including 2.9.0. It is fixed in 2.9.1.

The vulnerability is exploitable on Ruby implementations whose regular expression engine backtracks without memoization: MRI Ruby < 3.2 and JRuby. The second form, many-variable `+` and `#` expressions, is also exploitable on MRI Ruby 3.2, which does not memoize a regular expression that contains possessive quantifiers, and 2.9.0 generates those for these operators. It is also exploitable on TruffleRuby 40.0, whose regular expression engine falls back to backtracking for them. MRI Ruby 3.3 and later are not affected by any form, because they memoize those regular expressions too. TruffleRuby 40.0 is not affected by the other two forms. Earlier TruffleRuby versions were not tested.

This has been confirmed on the following runtimes with Addressable 2.9.0:

| Runtime | Status |
|---------|--------|
| MRI Ruby 2.7 | Vulnerable |
| MRI Ruby 3.1 | Vulnerable |
| MRI Ruby 3.2 | Vulnerable |
| MRI Ruby 3.3 | Not affected |
| MRI Ruby 3.4 | Not affected |
| MRI Ruby 4.0 | Not affected |
| JRuby 9.4 | Vulnerable |
| JRuby 10.1 | Vulnerable |
| TruffleRuby 40.0 | Vulnerable |

### Workarounds

- Upgrade to MRI Ruby 3.3 or later, if a consuming application does not use JRuby or TruffleRuby.
- Avoid matching user-supplied input on unpatched versions of the library against templates with several variables in one expression, or with several expressions next to each other.
- Apply a short timeout around any call to `Template#match` or `Template#extract` that processes user-supplied data.

### Credits

Reported by Matthew Mongeau (@halogenandtoast), Ruby Central Gem Security.

### For more information

If there are any questions or comments about this advisory:
* [Open an issue](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/issues)

raw.summary: rails-html-sanitizer: Possible regular expression denial of service with certain configurations
raw.details:
## Summary

`Rails::HTML::PermitScrubber` restricts the `href` and `xlink:href` attributes of SVG reference elements to local references. That check matched the attribute value against `/^\s*[^#\s].*/m`. In Ruby `^` anchors to every line start and `\s` matches newlines, so an all-whitespace value made the engine rescan the value from each of its line starts, taking time quadratic in its length.

- Versions affected: `>= 1.0.3, < 1.7.2`
- Not affected: `< 1.0.3`
- Fixed versions: `1.7.2`

Only Ruby 3.1 and earlier are affected. Ruby 3.2 added linear-time regexp matching, which makes the pattern linear.

## Impact

An attacker who supplies HTML to be sanitized can consume CPU out of proportion to the input size, by sending an SVG reference element whose `href` or `xlink:href` is a long run of whitespace.

Applications are affected only when the allowed tags are overridden to include an SVG reference element such as `use`, along with `href` or `xlink:href` in the allowed attributes. The default allowed tags include no SVG elements, so the default configuration is not affected. Applications that use Loofah directly are exposed through its own copy of the check, fixed in Loofah 2.25.3.

## Workarounds

Run Ruby 3.2 or later, which matches the pattern in linear time, or remove the SVG reference elements from the overridden allowed tags.

## Credit

Reported by scyoon through the Rails HackerOne program.

raw.summary: Active Storage: Possible arbitrary file write and read in image analysis
raw.details:
### Impact
A Rails application that processes attachments with ImageMagick may allow an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files on the server and, when attachments are stored with the Disk service, to read arbitrary files readable by the application process. Those files typically include `secret_key_base` and credentials for external systems, which may in turn allow escalation to remote code execution or lateral movement to those systems.

### Details
ImageMagick selects a coder from the content of the file it is given, and some coders act on files named inside the image rather than on the image itself. Active Storage constrained none of ImageMagick's coders, and the ImageMagick analyzer runs when a file is attached, so an attacker who can upload a crafted file may be able to invoke one. Attaching the upload is sufficient; no variant, preview, or `analyze` call is required. One specific attack chain has been reported to us, but we do not assume it is the only one that exists.

The fixed versions ship an ImageMagick security policy and prepend its directory to `MAGICK_CONFIGURE_PATH` through `MiniMagick.cli_env`, so every ImageMagick process that MiniMagick spawns applies it. The policy denies the `MSL` scripting coder, the coders that read or delete files other than the image, fetch remote or local references, or display to a screen, every coder backed by Ghostscript together with the `gs` delegate, and `@filename` indirection. ImageMagick applies every `policy.xml` on its search path, so the shipped policy adds to the host's policy rather than replacing it. The policy applies to every ImageMagick command that MiniMagick runs, not only those of Active Storage. See the `activestorage` CHANGELOG and "ImageMagick Security Policy" in the Active Storage guide.

### Affected applications
An application is affected if it meets all of these requirements:
- Uses ImageMagick for Active Storage image processing. This is `config.active_storage.variant_processor = :mini_magick`, which is the default for applications on `load_defaults 6.1` or earlier.
- Runs ImageMagick under a security policy that does not already deny the coders involved. The policies that Debian and Ubuntu package do not.
- Allows file uploads from untrusted users.

### Mitigation
- Upgrade to a fixed version of `activestorage`.
- An application whose variant processor is `:mini_magick` must use mini_magick `>= 5.1`, which applying the policy requires. With an older mini_magick, such an application raises an exception during boot.
- An application that renders PostScript or PDF through ImageMagick must re-allow the `gs` delegate and the coders it uses in the host's `policy.xml`.
- An application that replaces `MiniMagick.cli_env` after boot, clears the environment with `MiniMagick.cli_prefix`, or installs its own `MiniMagick::Shell` does not receive the shipped policy and must carry its rules in ImageMagick's system policy. GraphicsMagick does not read ImageMagick policies.
- If attachments are stored with the Disk service, change `secret_key_base` and every secret readable by the application process, including the master key and everything `config/credentials.yml.enc` holds, storage and database credentials, and third-party tokens. Do not retain an exposed secret as a fallback.

### Workarounds
Copy the rules of the policy that the fixed versions ship, `activestorage/lib/active_storage/image_magick/policy.xml`, into ImageMagick's system policy, for example `/etc/ImageMagick-7/policy.xml`. At a minimum, deny the `MSL` coder, the Ghostscript coders, and the `gs` delegate:

```xml
<policy domain="coder" rights="none" pattern="MSL"/>
<policy domain="delegate" rights="none" pattern="gs"/>
<policy domain="coder" rights="none" pattern="{PS,PS2,PS3,EPS,EPS2,EPS3,EPI,EPSF,EPSI,EPT,EPT2,EPT3,PDF,AI,EPDF,PDFA,POCKETMOD,XPS,PCL}"/>
```

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/468aa9a93fc98f5476b6821770f4ccfcb7f7d328
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/ea8c40121ce53a3d0255cd4eb6d13bfe3bc01776

### Versions affected
- activestorage < 8.0.5.2
- activestorage >= 8.1, < 8.1.4.1

### Credit
This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher [ryotak](https://hackerone.com/ryotak).

### References
- ImageMagick [security policy](https://imagemagick.org/security-policy/)

raw.summary: Action Pack: Missing SameSite attribute on session cookies from Action Pack session stores
raw.details:
### Impact
Action Pack session stores other than `ActionDispatch::Session::CookieStore` (`CacheStore`, `MemCacheStore`, and third-party stores built on `AbstractStore`, `AbstractSecureStore` or the session mixins) write the session cookie without a `SameSite` attribute, regardless of `config.action_dispatch.cookies_same_site_protection`, which defaults to `:lax`. Only `CookieStore` applies the configured policy. In browsers that do not treat a cookie without the attribute as `SameSite=Lax`, a cross-site request could carry the session cookie, possibly leading to cross-site request forgery against actions that do not verify an authenticity token, such as those of API-only applications.

Applications are affected when they use a session store other than `CookieStore` and do not pass `same_site:` to `config.session_store`.

### Details
In the fixed releases, every session store sets the session cookie's `SameSite` attribute from `cookies_same_site_protection` when its options have no `:same_site` key. An explicit `same_site:` option, including `same_site: nil`, and a `:same_site` value in a store's `DEFAULT_OPTIONS` still take precedence.

### Workarounds
Pass `same_site:` when configuring the session store, for example `config.session_store :cache_store, same_site: :lax`.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/2d9f502df941e31ce9bad0e846564f49396bed46.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/f2392996be723708271a8d30bfcf0edc221e53ef.patch

### Credit
This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher [tjvc](https://hackerone.com/tjvc).

raw.summary: Loofah: Mutation XSS in the HTML5 scrubbers through unescaped attribute values
raw.details:
## Summary

Loofah's HTML5 scrubbers could emit output that a browser parses into different markup, allowing mutation XSS. Nokogiri < 1.19.5 did not escape `<` and `>` in attribute values. When the output contained certain MathML, a browser treated markup inside an allowed attribute as live HTML. The `:strip` scrubber is affected in every browser. The `:prune` and `:escape` scrubbers are affected in WebKit browsers such as Safari.

Nokogiri 1.19.5 escapes `<` and `>` in attribute values, as the HTML standard requires. Loofah 2.25.3 requires Nokogiri >= 1.19.5.

## Impact

Applications that sanitize untrusted HTML with Loofah's HTML5 API (`Loofah.html5_fragment`, `Loofah.html5_document` and the `scrub_html5_*` methods) and display the result to other people are affected, including with the default allowlist.

Not affected: Loofah's HTML4 API (including `Loofah::Helpers.sanitize`), the `:whitewash` scrubber, rails-html-sanitizer's default configuration, and JRuby.

## Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3, or upgrade Nokogiri to >= 1.19.5.

raw.summary: rails-html-sanitizer: Possible XSS via shared scrubber state in concurrent calls
raw.details:
## Summary

`Rails::HTML::SafeListSanitizer` (both the HTML4 and HTML5 variants) shares one `Rails::HTML::PermitScrubber` across every `sanitize` call on the same instance, assigning its `tags` and `attributes` on each call without synchronization. Two concurrent `sanitize` calls with different `tags:` or `attributes:` options can interleave, so one call is scrubbed with the other call's allowlist.

- Versions affected: `< 1.7.2`
- Not affected: none
- Fixed versions: `1.7.2`

## Impact

Action View memoizes a single `SafeListSanitizer` per helper module and uses it for every `sanitize` call in the process, so in a multi-threaded server (for example Puma) all requests share the same `PermitScrubber`. If any code path calls `sanitize` with a more permissive allowlist, an attacker who can trigger that path concurrently with another request can cause the other request to be sanitized with the permissive allowlist. If the permissive allowlist admits `script` or an event-handler attribute, the strict call emits it unchanged, which is a cross-site scripting vector when the strict output is stored or rendered to other users.

Applications are affected only if they run more than one thread per process and some `sanitize` call passes `tags:` or `attributes:` options that differ from another call's, including a call that passes no options and so uses the defaults. Applications that use a single configuration everywhere, pass their own `scrubber:`, or run single-threaded are not affected.

## Workarounds

Use the same allowlist for every `sanitize` call, or pass a `scrubber:` built per call (`Rails::HTML::PermitScrubber.new` with `tags=` and `attributes=` set) instead of `tags:` and `attributes:` options.

## Credit

Reported by hiumee via HackerOne.

raw.summary: Active Storage: Possible circumvention of file size limits in Active Storage direct uploads to Google Cloud Storage
raw.details:
### Impact
`ActiveStorage::Service::GCSService#url_for_direct_upload` does not bind the declared content length into the signed direct-upload URL, and `#headers_for_direct_upload` returns no length constraint, so the URL authorizes an upload body of any size. A direct-upload client could store a file larger than the `byte_size` it declared, and the resulting blob keeps the declared size, possibly bypassing application file size validations and quotas. This is the weakness that CVE-2020-8162 fixed in the S3 service.

Applications that store files in Google Cloud Storage and accept direct uploads are affected.

### Details
The fixed releases sign an `x-goog-content-length-range` header that matches the blob's declared `byte_size` and return it from `headers_for_direct_upload`, so Cloud Storage rejects an upload body of any other size. Browsers send this header with the direct upload, so a bucket's CORS configuration must list `x-goog-content-length-range` in `responseHeader`, or browser direct uploads fail after the upgrade. The Active Storage CHANGELOG and the CORS example in the Active Storage guide show the change.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/e19916cea31cbfb0030b165ae853b741f8dd57a7.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/7fe85a72a789eae5ee070ce3ee1dad10a8a5f70c.patch

### Credit
This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher [f4cts](https://hackerone.com/f4cts).

raw.summary: Addressable: Regular Expression Denial of Service in templates with certain exploded expressions
raw.details:
### Impact

Within the URI template implementation in Addressable, templates using the `*` (explode) modifier with the `/`, `.`, `;`, `?` or `&` operators (e.g., `{/segments*}`, `{.ext*}`, `{;params*}`, `{?query*}`) generate regular expressions vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking. When `Template#match` or `Template#extract` is called with a maliciously crafted URI that starts with the operator's leading character, matching takes exponential time, leading to uncontrolled resource consumption and denial of service. An input under 60 bytes is enough to occupy a thread for minutes.

GHSA-h27x-rffw-24p4 (CVE-2026-35611) reported this pattern as fully remediated in 2.9.0. The 2.9.0 fix only made the joiner between exploded members mandatory for templates without an operator, and its regression specs used inputs that never start with the operator's leading character, so the vulnerable part of the expression was never reached. This issue was originally reported in #364 by @ebenoist in 2019 but insufficiently investigated.

Users of the URI parsing capabilities in Addressable but not the URI template matching capabilities are unaffected. Users who only call `Template#expand` are unaffected.

### Affected Versions

This vulnerability affects Addressable >= 2.3.0 (note: 2.3.0 and 2.3.1 were yanked; the earliest installable release is 2.3.2), including 2.9.0. It is fixed in 2.9.1.

The vulnerability is only exploitable on Ruby implementations whose regular expression engine backtracks without memoization: MRI Ruby < 3.2 and JRuby. MRI Ruby 3.2 and later are not affected: their regular expression engine memoizes backtracking, so these patterns still match in linear time. TruffleRuby 40.0 is not affected either. Earlier TruffleRuby versions were not tested.

This has been confirmed on the following runtimes with Addressable 2.9.0:

| Runtime | Status |
|---------|--------|
| MRI Ruby 2.7 | Vulnerable |
| MRI Ruby 3.1 | Vulnerable |
| MRI Ruby 3.2 | Not affected |
| MRI Ruby 3.3 | Not affected |
| MRI Ruby 3.4 | Not affected |
| MRI Ruby 4.0 | Not affected |
| JRuby 9.4 | Vulnerable |
| TruffleRuby 40.0 | Not affected |

### Workarounds

- Upgrade to MRI Ruby 3.2 or later, if the consuming application does not use JRuby.
- Avoid matching user-supplied input on unpatched versions of the library against templates that use the `*` modifier with the `/`, `.`, `;`, `?` or `&` operators.
- Apply a short timeout around any call to `Template#match` or `Template#extract` that processes user-supplied data.

### Credits

Reported independently by @ebenoist, @andrewstellman, and then @halogenandtoast.

### For more information

If there are any questions or comments about this advisory:
* [Open an issue](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable/issues)

raw.summary: Loofah allowed_uri? treats data:text/html as safe text/plain
raw.details:
## Summary

`Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.allowed_uri?` returns `true` for a `data:` URI whose mediatype is written with the HTML5 named character reference `/` in place of the solidus. Loofah reads that mediatype as malformed and falls back to the allowed `text/plain`, while a browser decodes the reference and reads the same URI as `text/html`.

## Details

`allowed_uri?` decodes HTML entities with `CGI.unescapeHTML`, which handles numeric character references but not HTML5 named character references. `/` therefore survives normalization, so the mediatype carries no `/`, fails the MIME grammar, and falls back to the allowed `text/plain` under the WHATWG rule for a malformed mediatype.

`:`, `/`, `	` and `
` are the only named character references in the HTML5 table that decode to characters that change how a URI parses (U+003A, U+002F, U+0009 and U+000A; there is no named reference for U+000D), so this closes the set.

Loofah's default `sanitize()` path is **not** affected, because Nokogiri decodes the entity during parsing before Loofah evaluates the URI. This issue affects only callers of the public `allowed_uri?` string-level helper that pass it HTML-encoded strings.

## Impact

Applications that validate a user-controlled URL with `Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.allowed_uri?` and then render the approved value into an `href` or another browser-interpreted URI attribute may be vulnerable to cross-site scripting. `Rails::HTML::Sanitizer.allowed_uri?` re-exports the same helper.

## Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3.

## Credit

Responsibly reported by GitHub user @ngpestelos.

raw.summary: Loofah: CSS url() sanitization bypass via escaped parentheses
raw.details:
## Summary

`Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.scrub_css` rejected any property whose top-level Crass tokens included a `:url` or `:bad_url`, and left `url` out of the allowed CSS functions. Both checks ran only against the first parse of the `style` attribute. When `scrub_css` rebuilt each property it emitted identifiers with their CSS escapes decoded, so parentheses written as escapes — `url\28 …\29` — hid the `url` token from the checks, and the rebuilt value was re-parsed into a live `url()` that nothing checked again. An escaped property name, six-digit escapes, escaped comments and escaped quotes all reached the same place.

## Impact

A sanitized `style` attribute could make a viewer's browser issue a request to an attacker-chosen URL. `list-style` fetches on render with no interaction, `cursor` on hover. That leaks the viewer's IP address, user agent and access timing, and can reach hosts routable only from the viewer's network. No script survives sanitization and the attacker cannot read the response, so the request itself is the whole impact.

Applications that sanitize user-supplied HTML with Loofah's default allowlist and display it to other people are affected.

## Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3.

## Credit

Reported by NotAFlightRisk through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting.

raw.summary: Loofah: Regular expression denial of service in the SVG local-reference check
raw.details:
## Summary

Loofah's HTML5 sanitizer restricts the `href` and `xlink:href` attributes of SVG reference elements to local references. That check matched the attribute value against `/^\s*[^#\s].*/m`. In Ruby `^` anchors to every line start and `\s` matches newlines, so an all-whitespace value made the engine rescan the value from each of its line starts, taking time quadratic in its length.

Only Ruby 3.1 and earlier are affected. Ruby 3.2 added linear-time regexp matching, which makes the pattern linear.

## Impact

An attacker who supplies HTML to be sanitized can consume CPU out of proportion to the input size, by sending an SVG reference element whose `href` or `xlink:href` is a long run of whitespace.

The default safelist allows the elements in `SVG_ALLOW_LOCAL_HREF`, so no configuration change is required.

## Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3. Applications that cannot upgrade should run Ruby 3.2 or later, which matches the pattern in linear time.

## Credit

Reported by scyoon through the Rails HackerOne program.

raw.summary: Active Storage: Possible DoS vulnerability in Active Storage filename handling
raw.details:
### Impact
`ActiveStorage::Filename#base` and `#extension_with_delimiter`, and therefore `#extension`, pass the stored filename unmodified to `File.basename` and `File.extname`, which raise `ArgumentError` when the name contains a NUL byte. Active Storage stores the client-supplied filename verbatim, so a user who is permitted to upload an attachment could persist such a filename on databases that accept NUL bytes in string columns, such as SQLite and MySQL/MariaDB. Each subsequent request that builds a variant or preview of the blob, opens it, or renders it as an Action Text attachment then raises, possibly resulting in a persistent DoS vulnerability for the pages that display the blob until it is purged or its filename is corrected. Applications that use PostgreSQL are not affected, because PostgreSQL rejects the row.

### Details
`Filename#base` and `#extension_with_delimiter` now derive from `Filename#sanitized`, the form that `Filename#to_s` and the `Content-Disposition` header already use. For a filename that `#sanitized` changes, such as one containing a NUL byte, an invalid byte sequence, a path separator or another replaced character, the base and extension now agree with `#to_s`; the variant format inferred from such a name may change, and an existing variant may be regenerated once. Stored filenames are not modified, and no data migration is required.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/60f22af88b71eae251f112d8c0237a08a8832692.patch
- 8.0: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/9b0d4bef2211a2c08cab2e0ea17fa1d0efd5d47a.patch

### Credit
This issue was found by the Anthropic OSS Scanner (ANT-2026-UQM5Z4YL).

raw.summary: Loofah allowed_uri? treats javascript&#x3a alert(1) as safe
raw.details:
## Summary

`Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.allowed_uri?` returns `true` for a `javascript:` or `vbscript:` URI whose scheme is split by a numeric character reference without a trailing semicolon, followed by a character that `allowed_uri?` strips, such as a space or tab. A browser ends the reference at that character and reads `javascript&#x3a alert(1)` as `javascript: alert(1)`.

## Details

`allowed_uri?` strips control characters and whitespace before it decodes numeric character references. Removing the character that ends a semicolon-less reference lets the reference run on into the following text, so `&#x3a alert` decodes as `&#x3aa` (U+03AA) instead of a colon, and no scheme is detected. The same applies to decimal references and to references that encode a scheme letter, as in `&#x6a\tavascript:alert(1)`.
